steps.objective: Independent read-only review of G1 evidence (closes the self-attestation gap)
steps.outcome: 17 findings accepted, several of which corrected this evidence set

steps.objective: Formal G1 gate report with content digests, per doc 11 line 51
steps.outcome: result FAIL; 8 of 9 criteria supported, domain tests unsupported

steps.objective: Audit 0002_market_data.sql for documented-but-unenforced controls
steps.outcome: 16a-16d; 16c deliberately left open

steps.objective: Implement + mutation-test G2 structural gaps as migration 0019
Close the Go/PostgreSQL canonical-ID parity gap (0020)
steps.outcome: Two encoders agreed on format and disagreed on values. Now pinned by 8 vectors x 29 entity types.

steps.objective: Bind the nanosecond/TIMESTAMPTZ pair and correct the reversed 0009 decision (0021)
steps.outcome: Defects 19 and 20. Binding exposed three two-clock fixtures and a void-in-CHECK constraint that was always false.

steps.objective: Replace self-invalidating inline evidence digests with a generated manifest + verifier
steps.outcome: Drift, missing-file and unlisted-file all fail nonzero; both failure modes exercised in both directions.

steps.objective: Implement the domain packages that G1 criterion 9 requires, with Go/SQL parity and mutation testing
steps.outcome: 78 unit tests + 6 parity tests, mutation tested 11/11. Defects 21-23 found and fixed, including a test that passed while asserting nothing.

steps.objective: Make the risk gate a projection of risk.policy rather than an invented limit model, and pin it to the schema
steps.outcome: Defects 24-26. Three INTEGER limit columns were set-but-never-consulted because the rate control took a pre-computed bool. The policy's permitted_instruments/venues allowlists were unread, so a restrictive policy behaved unconditionally. risk.Policy replaced an invented generic limit model that had never been compared to the schema.

steps.objective: Load risk.policy from PostgreSQL and close the recorded gap that the gate had never approved an order in a real configuration
steps.outcome: Defects 27-30. An order is now approved by a gate running on a committed policy row, with paired denials per limit. Found: pgx stdlib returns text[] as a literal string so []string scan fails at runtime; interval parsing left the plural 's' behind on '2 days'; array Value() lost double quotes; committed test rows outlived their test and shadowed later runs.

steps.objective: Stop the risk gate measuring numbers its caller asserted: source account, position and strategy state from the database
steps.outcome: Defects 31-33 and 35. Build computed AccountAuthorized and StrategyDeployed and then discarded them, so both controls reported 'not evaluated'; it left a caller's asserted concentration in place for a flat book while stamping provenance as if this package had sourced it; the integration fixture asserted leverage 1.2 and drawdown 0.05 as Go literals while reading nothing; and Load accepted a caller-asserted read stamp. The fixture now builds instruments, orders, validated fills and positions in a rolled-back transaction, because the schema refuses a position no validated fill implies.

steps.objective: Source instrument eligibility and precision validity from market.instrument instead of caller booleans
steps.outcome: Defects 36-38. riskstate.Load now calls instrument.Evaluate for every order and overwrites the caller's InstrumentEligible and PrecisionValid rather than consulting them; the fixture no longer asserts either. Defect 36 was contracts.Decimal.Div computing a*10^guard/b and ignoring the difference between the operands' scales, so it was correct only when both carried the same scale -- 1/0.1 returned 1, and both risk ratios divide unlike scales, so max_drawdown and max_concentration were being compared against a corrupted figure; at unequal scales the old code crossed the 'above 1' guard and errored, so the measurement could not be taken at all. Defect 37: risk.OrderFacts had no Side, which nothing needed while eligibility was a caller boolean, and instrument.Permits keys its shorting check on side == 'SELL' -- so a missing side would have passed straight through it and a long-only instrument would have permitted a short. Defect 38: instrument.Permits now refuses a side that is neither BUY nor SELL instead of falling through the shorting check. 6 new database tests, mutation 7/7.

steps.objective: Compose the complete risk gate from persisted authorities and source halts from ops.halt
steps.outcome: Defects 39-41. domain/gate is the single entry point that submits order terms, derives the risk-reducing predicate from OrderType.RiskIncreasing, resolves policy and reads halts from committed rows, and takes transactional account, position, strategy and instrument state through riskstate.Querier. Defect 39: gate.Evaluate passed risk.HaltDecision{Evaluated: true} -- a literal asserting that halts had been checked, which is the same class of defect as the caller-asserted booleans in S11 and S12; halts are now loaded from ops.halt. Defect 40: MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL was unreachable, because OrderFacts.Notional was left to the caller and then overwritten with nil by riskstate.Build, so the control compared a limit against an unset pointer and could not refuse anything. Notional is now derived from the order's own quantity and price, and deliberately left nil for a market order, which correctly denies rather than approximating a value it does not have. Defect 41: the composed gate had never been run, so nothing had ever checked that policy, halts, account, position, strategy and instrument state coexist. 7 composition tests. The mutation proof found the first halt mutant unreached -- disabling the early return left the suite green because the post-load recheck enforces halts independently -- so the meaningful mutant disables both enforcement points.

steps.objective: Pin the risk gate's control enumeration and the halt hierarchy to doc 04, so completeness is checked rather than asserted
steps.outcome: The gate implements exactly doc 04's 15 mandatory checks in doc 04's order, and that mapping existed only as a prose comment. domain/risk/doc04_test.go parses the bullet list out of doc 04 at test time and asserts a 1:1 ordered mapping to Controls(); it also ties the consumes flag to RequiresLimit so the two claims about which controls take a number cannot drift apart. domain/halt/doc04_test.go reads the SYSTEM_HALT > ... > ACCOUNT_HALT chain out of doc 04 and asserts Levels() matches it strongest-first, plus total ordering. The limit direction was already covered: TestColumnsWithNoDoc04Control pins exactly which of the 12 policy columns have no control, and TestTheGateEvaluatesExactlyDoc04sFifteenControls pinned the count -- what was missing was the identity and order of the 15. Mutation 2/2: removing LOSS_AND_DRAWDOWN_CONTROL from the enumeration and MARKET_HALT from the hierarchy are each caught. Both new tests fail rather than skip when doc 04 is unreadable, because a skip would leave the gate unpinned in exactly the environment where the specification is missing.

steps.objective: Pin the four OMS closed vocabularies to their PostgreSQL enums, and collapse four copies of the risk-reducing classification into one
steps.outcome: Defects 42-44. The transition rules were pinned to oms.state_transition_rule but the vocabularies they are written in were not, which is why the divergence in defect 42 could persist. Four spellings of the risk-reducing set existed: contracts.OrderType.RiskIncreasing (9 members, matching the database, and the one domain/gate actually calls), a package-local oms.OrderType.RiskReducing (6 members, missing POST_ONLY/IOC/FOK, documented as 'the same predicate migration 0013 uses at the risk boundary' and cited by domain/instrument, with no consumer outside its own test), a bool field on risk.OrderFacts, and domain/instrument's own closing() comparing two literals. The oms copy is deleted rather than corrected -- a second implementation of the same predicate is the defect, not its member set -- instrument now delegates to contracts, and the parity test reads contracts. Defect 43: IOC and FOK appear in both common.order_type and common.time_in_force, and oms.order carried both columns NOT NULL with no constraint preventing a contradictory pair such as order_type='IOC', time_in_force='GTC'. 0022 forbids them in oms.order.order_type, chosen over dropping the enum values because instrument.order_types and policy.permitted_order_types are arrays of that enum and may legitimately list them as venue capabilities. Defect 44: two of the fourteen event kinds (SUBMIT_FAILED, CANCEL_REQUESTED) drive no transition at all, which is legitimate but was not recorded anywhere; it is now pinned by name. 9 new parity tests. Mutation 2/2: dropping the 0022 constraint from the live schema and adding a value to contracts' closed set are each caught, the second by both the new parity test and the pre-existing gate test.

steps.objective: Build the OMS orchestrator: drive an order from RISK_APPROVED to a venue outcome, and enforce the no-retry-after-UNKNOWN rule that only a sequencing layer can enforce
steps.outcome: Defects 45-46. and doc 01 invariant 3 require that no exposure-increasing retry follow an undetermined submission outcome, and nothing enforced it. The venue adapter cannot (it caused the timeout), the risk gate cannot (it evaluates an unsubmitted order), and no constraint can (a CHECK sees one row, not the attempt history). domain/execution enforces it over an attempt history carried with each request. SubmissionRequest.PreviousAttempts is a required field with no default so a caller who forgets to load the history gets a compile error rather than a silent resubmission. Defect 46: my first draft recorded RISK_APPROVED -> ACKNOWLEDGED as a single move, which the closed set does not permit -- doc 04 puts SUBMITTING between RISK_APPROVED and every venue outcome. The state machine caught it; the fix records two transitions, and SUBMITTING is recorded before the venue is called so the interval between leaving the platform's control and learning the outcome is visible in the journal rather than indistinguishable from an order that was never sent. The risk decision id is threaded per call rather than fixed on the submitter, because both the RISK_APPROVED -> SUBMITTING and SUBMITTING -> ACKNOWLEDGED rules carry RequiresRiskDecision and a reused submitter would otherwise carry one order's decision into another's journal. Resolve is a separate method on a separate interface from Submit: resolution is a read of venue state, and conflating the two is how a reconciliation becomes an accidental second order. 18 tests. Mutation 1/1: disabling the no-retry guard fails TestASecondSubmissionIsRefusedAfterAnUndeterminedOutcome and TestARefusedRetryRecordsNothing.

steps.objective: Make the durable exit from UNKNOWN, then delete the superseded in-memory Submitter so there is exactly one door to each operation
steps.outcome:
Defects 47-49. The durable exit from UNKNOWN was missing, and it was the last behaviour living only in the retired Submitter, which had no durable path at all: it wrote its transition through a Recorder interface and kept the attempt history in a slice the caller supplied. domain/execution/resolve.go implements Command.Resolve against execution.submission and oms.order_event. The operation order is deliberate -- read durable history and refuse unless something is undetermined, THEN ask the venue, THEN commit outcome and transition together. The precondition is read before the network call so a caller is never billed a venue query for an order with nothing to resolve; a test asserts the fake resolver's call count is zero in that case. Defect 47: the submission row is rewritten in place rather than appended. Appending would present one send as two attempts, which is exactly the counting the no-blind-retry rule depends on, so a resolved order would read as a retry. Defect 48: Command.Resolve initially returned a hardcoded State of ACKNOWLEDGED while the transaction correctly wrote REJECTED. The database caught the lie and TestResolvingToARejectionUnblocksTheOrder failed on it; commitResolution now returns the state it committed, because returning an intended value would let a caller act on a transition the database never accepted. Defect 49: commitResolution mutated state with no audit record and no outbox row. Doc 05 requires an outbox row for every committed state mutation and doc 22 requires policy_version on every audit record, and neither is enforced by a trigger, so the omission was silent. Both are now written in the command's transaction, and enqueue was refactored from a SubmitIntent-shaped helper into a neutral outboxEnvelope so Prepare and Resolve express the obligation through one statement rather than two that can drift. The actor is required rather than defaulted to a component name, because doc 21 forbids service identities impersonating humans and a resolution with no accountable actor cannot be audited. policy_version is read from the order's own risk_policy_revisions rather than from the caller or a constant, and an order with no recorded revision is REFUSED rather than resolved with a placeholder -- an order that cleared the risk gate without recording the policy that admitted it has an evidence gap, and adding another record to that chain would bury it.

An unrecognised venue answer, and a venue that cannot be asked, both leave the order in UNKNOWN. Adopting an answer the platform cannot interpret would end the order's life at exactly the moment it knows least, which is the failure oms.State.Terminal's comment warns about for UNKNOWN specifically. Resolution cannot place an order: the venue side is the Resolver interface, which declares Resolve and nothing else, so a submit-capable adapter cannot be passed as a resolver without the compiler noticing.

Then the Submitter was deleted rather than repaired (defect 50). With both Submit and Resolve durable, it was fully redundant, and it was the second and weaker door to the same operation: its history was whatever the caller passed, so the no-retry rule could be bypassed by passing an empty slice; it held no durable record, so an order could move with nothing committed to account for it; and it offered a second Resolve that did exactly what the new one does without the durability. Two implementations of a money-affecting lifecycle operation, one of them silently non-durable, is the hazard this package exists to prevent. It also took the obsolete Venue and Recorder interfaces with it -- submission is outbox-driven now, so a venue call is made by a dispatcher reading committed rows rather than by an in-process interface, and audit goes through audit.Appender. The pure vocabulary it shared (Outcome, Attempt, UndeterminedPrior, the three outcomes, both errors) moved to vocabulary.go; its 18 tests went with it, and every invariant they covered is asserted durably instead: TestAPreparedSubmitRefusesWhenDurableHistoryIsUndetermined, TestASecondAttemptWithoutReconciliationIsRefusedBeforeWriting, TestASecondAttemptWithReconciliationIsRecordedAsAttemptTwo, TestATimedOutSubmissionIsUndeterminedAndBlocksTheNextSend, TestAResolvedTimeoutStopsBlocking, and TestABlindRetryIsRefusedByGoAndByTheDatabase. Attempt numbering moved to dbtest with the rows it describes. One test was kept in rewritten form.

11 new integration tests in dbtest/resolve_test.go against the live tables. Mutation 3/3, all re-established after the deletion: disabling Prepare's undetermined-attempt guard fails TestAPreparedSubmitRefusesWhenDurableHistoryIsUndetermined; disabling Resolve's nothing-to-resolve guard fails TestResolvingAnOrderWithNoUndeterminedAttemptIsRefused; mislabelling the resolution's outbox event_type fails TestResolvingLeavesAnAuditRecordAndAnOutboxRow. A first attempt at the second mutant reported green and was wrong -- the replacement string did not match, so the file was unchanged and nothing was mutated. A mutation that does not apply proves exactly as little as one that fails to compile, and the tell was the same.

Two incidental findings. risk_policy_revisions is a text[] and pgx v5 through database/sql hands it back as a literal string, so scanning it into []string fails at runtime -- the same driver behaviour already recorded for the permitted_* columns, and now handled by having SQL return the last element directly rather than by adding a second Scanner. And any code deriving a nanosecond count from a time.Time must truncate to microseconds first, because the audit appender derives occurred_at_ns from OccurredAt while PostgreSQL stores timestamptz at microsecond resolution; Prepare relies on its caller to truncate, and Resolve truncates the timestamp it mints itself because it cannot check a discipline it does not own.

steps.objective: Build the outbox dispatcher that turns a committed outbox row into a venue call, and close the file-order-dependent id collision it exposed in the shared test fixtures
steps.outcome:
Defect 51. services/dispatch/dispatch.go reads ops.outbox, claims a batch under a lease, routes each row to a registered Publisher and records the outcome. This is the caller the ledger said was missing: Command.Prepare and Command.Resolve were both durable and both proven, and nothing invoked either in a running path.

Attempt accounting was the part that had to be right. A claim does NOT increment attempt_count and the publisher is handed Attempt = attempt_count + 1, so a successful publication leaves the count unchanged and only a failure spends an attempt. Incrementing on claim would charge every message an attempt whether or not it was ever sent, making the ceiling a ceiling on claims rather than on sends. ErrUnroutable is permanent rather than transient, so an event type with no publisher dead-letters immediately instead of consuming the retry budget on a fact that cannot change. A claim whose lease expired at its final attempt is dead-lettered LEASE_EXPIRED_EXHAUSTED rather than left DISPATCHING, because outbox_exhausted_is_dead_lettered refuses an exhausted row in any other state and it would otherwise be stranded with no attempt left to reclaim it. Publisher is required to be idempotent by EventID per doc 05.

Defect 52. Found by the dispatcher, but not in the dispatcher: adding dbtest/dispatch_test.go broke 13 unrelated tests across gate_composition_test.go, invariants_test.go and risk_gate_integration_test.go, every one on a duplicate-key error, and none in the dispatcher's own behaviour.

dbtest.CanonicalID derives its value from (prefix, n, runNonce), so n alone is the entire collision surface. readyOrder COMMITs the ids it mints, because the ledger and journal tables are append-only and a test that observes a real commit cannot delete its rows afterwards. That counter started at 1 -- the same space as the literal ids those files hardcode, such as ins 11 and acc 3 -- so dispatch_test.go, sorting under 'd' ahead of 'g' and 'i', claimed literals that later files still meant to use. The usable range had been a property of FILE ORDER, which made adding any test file in the first half of the alphabet a latent way to break the suite.

A/B proof, because the failure implicated thirteen tests and exonerated none of them: with dispatch_test.go moved out of the build the package was 333 pass / 0 fail; with it in place, 325 pass / 20 fail. seq() now counts from 1000000, above the largest literal used anywhere in the package (970500) and above the 900000+ band risk_gate_integration_test.go reserves, which makes the two ranges disjoint by construction rather than by alphabet. dbtest.UniqueSequence could not collide either; it already returns values at or above 1<<31. Three consecutive full runs after the fix: 345 pass / 0 fail, with go build ./... and go vet ./... clean.

steps.objective: Give the dispatcher unit tests over its database-independent surface, and fix the clock-derived sequence collision that running the suite repeatedly exposed
steps.outcome:
Two defects, only one of which is about the dispatcher.

First, the dispatcher's database-independent surface had no coverage at all. All 12 of its tests live in dbtest/dispatch_test.go and need the live database, so the code that runs before or instead of a query was untested. services/dispatch/dispatch_test.go now covers truncate, the constructor refusals, the fluent setters, the clock seam and the ErrUnroutable sentinel: 8 tests, 22 including subtests.

truncate is the one that mattered. It is the only function in the package that transforms text on its way into a column a human reads, and it makes an explicit claim that cutting mid-rune produces invalid UTF-8, which PostgreSQL would refuse to store in a text column -- a failure that would arrive as a dead-letter write aborting, which is the worst possible moment to discover a string-length bug. That claim was asserted in a comment and checked by nothing. Venue error bodies are not short ASCII, so the multi-byte cases are the ones that occur. The test also records that the bound applies to the retained prefix and not to the result length, since the marker is added on top; that looks like a defect and is not, so it is now pinned rather than left to be "tidied". Mutation 6/6: removing the rune-boundary walk, changing <= to <, weakening either setter guard, deleting the name check and neutering withClock are each caught. Every mutation also asserts the anchor changed, because the restore in that harness is itself where defect 54 came from.

Second, and not about the dispatcher at all: dbtest.UniqueSequence was not unconditionally unique. It derived its run multiplier from a nanosecond clock as (runNonce & 0x3fffffff) % 100000, which lands on 0 about once in a hundred thousand runs, and when it does run*base vanishes and the function returns exactly n. So a test asking for a unique sequence received 1, 2, 3 -- the same values other tests hardcode.

The consequence was permanent rather than transient. ledger.entry.sequence is globally unique and append-only, so a committed row on sequence 1 can never be removed. It was found here as a committed TRADE_CASH/FEE journal pair sitting on sequences 1 and 2, which made TestLedgerUpdateAndDeleteAreRejected and TestInternalLedgerEntryMustBelongToAJournal fail on ledger_entry_sequence_idx for every subsequent run. The evidence that it was the multiplier and not something else: every other committed journal pair in the database has a distinct non-zero implied multiplier (1476, 21320, 24232, 24372, 40396, 41660, 44096, 58144, 59628, 61684, 70864) and exactly one pair implies multiplier 0, recorded during this session. Those two rows are the only TRADE_CASH 1 / FEE 2 pair any code path produces, and the only source of the values 1 and 2 for it is UniqueSequence returning bare n.

UniqueSequence now returns run*base + n + sequenceFloor, with the floor at 1000000, which puts the lowest possible result above every sequence literal in the suite. dbtest/sequence_namespace_test.go exercises the degenerate case on every run instead of once in a hundred thousand, by setting the run nonce through the exported SetRunNonce and restoring it afterwards. Mutation: removing the floor is caught by TestUniqueSequenceNeverReturnsALiteral and TestUniqueSequenceCollidesWithAnotherCoincidentalRun.

The floor does NOT make two coincidental runs unique, and the tests say so rather than implying otherwise. Two runs whose nonces share a masked multiplier still collide with each other, because the multiplier is the only input that varies. What changes is the severity: before, a coincidence poisoned an append-only table permanently and broke unrelated tests forever; now it produces a duplicate-key failure inside the two runs that actually share sequences, which is self-diagnosing and cleared by a reset.

The poisoned database was cleared with the suite's own documented prerequisite, db/migrate.ps1 -Container aitc-pg17 -Reset: applied_now=22 total_files=22 failures=0 drift=0, ledger.entry back to 0 rows. Two consecutive full runs after the reset are 831 pass / 0 fail, with gofmt, go build and go vet clean across the repository.

steps.objective: Build the ledger poster: commit a balanced double-entry posting with its journal header, audit record and outbox row in one transaction, and make a retried posting provably incapable of moving money twice
steps.outcome:
Defects 55-57, and one schema property that shapes the whole design.

domain/ledger/poster.go posts a balanced journal. Doc 05 requires domain validation, state mutation, audit record and outbox insertion in one transaction, and the poster composes all four: ledger.journal, every ledger.entry, the audit record, and ops.outbox. An entry committed without its audit record would assert a movement the evidence trail does not corroborate, and ledger_entry_append_only means that assertion can never be withdrawn.

Defect 55, and it was nearly invisible. Amounts are NUMERIC(38,18), so a stored 1 comes back from PostgreSQL as '1.000000000000000000'. The first draft of the replay check compared committed amounts to the caller's amount as text, which would have reported ErrReplayConflict on EVERY replay of a perfectly good posting -- and would have done so with a message claiming two different postings claimed the same identity, sending the operator to investigate a contradiction that did not exist. The check compares contracts.Decimal values now, and TestReplayingAPostingIsIdempotent is what pins it: the poster has no test double, so the only way to know is against the real column.

Defect 56. The same scale has a second consequence, on the write side rather than the read side: submitting 19 decimal places would be rounded by the column, posting an amount other than the one the caller asked for while the audit record carried the caller's figure. An amount finer than storageScale is now refused before the transaction opens.

Defect 57. Replay suppression is content-addressed, which means a PARTIAL overlap is a new failure mode rather than a replay. If two of a posting's four digests are already committed and two are not, the ledger holds part of a posting. Completing it would assert a journal it never accepted whole; posting it fresh would move money the committed legs already moved. Neither is attempted: the poster refuses, names how many legs were found, and writes nothing. The test appends legs rather than altering an amount on purpose, because an altered amount is caught by the balance check first and never reaches the replay path this test exists to cover.

Replay is keyed on source_digest, which is UNIQUE (ledger_entry_source_digest_idx) and was therefore already the database's own idempotency key. Each digest is sha256 over a unit-separated pre-image of command, account, currency, kind, direction, amount, effective instant and the leg's INDEX in the posting. The index is included because entry ids are minted per attempt; without it two orderings of the same legs collide, and TestLegDigestsAreStableAndOrderSensitive pins both the stability and the order-sensitivity.

The schema property: ledger.journal_must_balance looks up the header by (journal_id, account_id, currency) and raises foreign_key_violation when no header matches the leg. Every leg of a journal therefore has to carry its header's account AND currency. That is why Posting holds Currency and AccountID once rather than per leg, and it is a genuine limitation worth stating rather than discovering: this schema cannot express a two-account transfer in one journal, and a journal whose legs are not balanced to zero cannot exist at all. TRANSFER exists in ledger.entry_kind but cannot be balanced within a single account.

Sequence allocation takes pg_advisory_xact_lock before reading max(sequence)+1. ledger_entry_sequence_idx is UNIQUE across the whole ledger rather than per account, so two postings for different accounts still collide; without the lock both could read max+1 and one would fail on the index at COMMIT, long after its caller had been told nothing.

Two things the poster refuses rather than defaults, both discovered by running it against the database rather than by reading the schema. audit.record.signing_key_id is NOT NULL, so an unsigned record is representable: NewPoster now takes a signing key and refuses an empty one, because an empty string satisfies the column while naming no key at all. And every audit partition row carries CHECK (length(policy_version) > 0), so PolicyVersion is a required field on Posting, supplied by the caller for the same reason the OMS submit command does not invent one.

Tests: 8 top-level / 25 including subtests in domain/ledger, 6 top-level / 10 including subtests in dbtest/ledger_posting_test.go. TestPostingCommitsHeaderEntriesAuditAndOutboxTogether asserts all four artifacts and then calls ledger.verify_journal, so the header-agrees-with-its-entries verdict is the constraint's own rather than a reimplementation of it. TestAnUnbalancedPostingIsRefusedBeforeItIsWritten asserts both that the refusal names both totals and that zero entries exist afterwards.

One test-design defect worth recording, because it produced a convincing wrong answer rather than an obvious failure. dbtest.UniqueSequence is a pure function of n: every test that asks for sequence 1 gets the SAME id. The first version of this file had three tests each call tradePosting(t) with no seed, so all three shared a SourceCommandID, and the row-count assertions were counting each other's committed rows. It surfaced as 'the replay posted again' when the replay had in fact been suppressed, and as 'the refusal still wrote' when nothing had been written. The fixture now takes a seed and each test takes a distinct block, which is the same lesson as defects 52 and 53: on this suite, an id counter shared between files is a latent way to break an unrelated test.

steps.objective: Define the venue capability and certification contract, and make every certification check fail closed
steps.outcome:
adapters/venue/contract.go declares the 12 capabilities, the adapter declaration and registry, the six certification states, the environment permissions, and the venue order, fill, balance, position, request and result models that Reader, Writer, Mapper and Adapter are built from. The capability constants are the 12 CHECK literals in execution.adapter_capability, and dbtest/venue_capability_parity_test.go reads that constraint out of the live catalog and asserts the Go set matches it in both directions, so a capability added to either side alone fails the build rather than becoming a value the gate silently refuses.

adapters/venue/gate.go resolves a real certification and fails closed on every gap rather than on a default. Missing declaration, missing certification row, provenance mismatch against the declaration, an unsupported capability, an expired certification, and each of the non-certified states are all refusals. This is the choice that matters most in the file: an absent row could have been read as uncertified-but-harmless, and instead it is exactly as disqualifying as a revoked certificate, because the only way to obtain a row is a deliberate act by a person who accepted a certification agreement.

stateFor returns Uncertified for an absent declaration rather than guessing, and a removed certification state is refused rather than defaulted. The other direction is the hazard: a default for a state the code does not recognise would let a future REVOKED-LIKE state pass. Both directions are pinned by name rather than left to a reader's assumption.

steps.objective: Wire the certification gate into OMS submission, after finding that the gate had been referenced only by its own tests
steps.outcome:
The finding that shaped this step: the certification gate existed, was correct, and gated nothing. It was constructed in tests and never in a production path, so an uncertified adapter could have had an order prepared and submitted with no certification check anywhere on the route. A control that only its own tests exercise is a control that does not exist.

The interface is declared in the consumer rather than the implementer. domain/execution declares SubmissionGate and never imports adapters, because domain importing its own adapter is the inversion that makes a test double impossible to write and a package cycle inevitable. adapters/venue/submission_gate.go implements it and carries a compile-time assertion that it satisfies the declaration, so the two cannot drift without a build failure.

Making the gate unavoidable rather than merely available was the part that needed the design. NewCommand now takes a SubmissionGate and refuses a nil one with ErrNoSubmissionGate, so there is no constructor path that yields a Command capable of preparing an order without a certification authority behind it. SubmitIntent.AdapterID became a required field for the same reason: a submission that does not name its adapter cannot be certified, and an empty string has no certification to look up.

PermitSubmit runs before BeginTx, so a refusal leaves the order at RISK_APPROVED and writes no submission, no audit record and no outbox row. Checking it inside the transaction would have been equally correct but would have opened a transaction only to roll it back. 8 integration tests cover uncertified, expired, paper/live mismatch, revoked, unsupported capability, undeclared adapter, the positive case, and revocation between two requests, and each refusal asserts the order state, the absence of a submission row and the absence of an outbox row rather than only that an error came back.

steps.objective: Re-check certification at the dispatcher's send site, because a certificate valid at Prepare can be withdrawn before the order leaves
steps.outcome:
S22 closed the gap between a certification and an order being prepared. This step closed the one after it. Prepare and the venue call are separated by a commit, a claim and a lease, and a person can withdraw a certification in that interval, so a check at Prepare alone would authorise a send on the strength of a certificate that no longer exists. The send site re-checks, and the two checks are deliberately not the same call site: one is a precondition and one is the last thing before the order leaves the platform.

adapters/venue.SubmitPublisher is the thing that turns a committed outbox row into a venue call, and it is the first code in this repository that can place a real order. services/dispatch imports only contracts, so the publisher introduces no import cycle; the venue call stays outside the authoritative transaction, because holding a database transaction open across a network call to a third party is how a connection pool runs out under load.

The publisher returns nil after a successful venue call even when recording the answer fails. That is deliberate and it is the most important line in the file. Returning the recording error would make the dispatcher treat the publication as failed and call the venue again, and the second call is a second live order. A recording failure is recoverable and a duplicate order is not, so the submission is left PENDING, which is precisely the undetermined state the no-blind-retry CHECK refuses to send again until a human reconciles it. TestAFailedRecordingAfterTheSendIsNotRetried exists to hold that line, and it asserts the venue call count is exactly 1 rather than asserting only that no error came back.

Every refusal in this file is asserted the same way: the writer's call count is zero. An error returned after a send would satisfy a weaker test and would be the duplicate-order failure this path exists to prevent, so counting calls is the assertion that carries the meaning. 9 integration tests against the live tables.

Undetermined outcomes are never rejections, in all four forms the venue can produce them in. A timeout, a transport error, an error payload and a state the adapter's StateMap does not recognise all become UNKNOWN with reason TIMED_OUT_UNKNOWN, because in each case the platform cannot distinguish a request that was rejected on arrival from one that was placed, and recording REJECTED would durably assert that no exposure exists on the strength of a value it does not understand. An unmapped state is the sharpest case: the venue has invented a value the adapter has never seen, and reading it as anything is a guess. An instrument with no effective market.venue_symbol mapping is not sent at all, because guessing a symbol is how an order reaches the wrong instrument.

The venue.Writer in these tests is a recording double, and that is the real remaining gap: there is no concrete adapter for any venue in this repository. TestACertifiedAdapterIsSentAndTheOrderIsAcknowledged proves the send path reaches a writer with the order's own side, quantity and audited venue symbol and that the order leaves SUBMITTING, but it proves it against a double. A real venue cannot be certified against a test double, so adapters/venue and the reconciliation runner are the two open items on G3.

steps.objective: Execute reconciliation, because a submission that can become UNKNOWN is only safe if something resolves it
steps.outcome:
Four checks -- orders, fills, balances, positions -- and each is COMPLETED, SKIPPED or FAILED. Never silently clean. A check whose capability the adapter is not certified for is SKIPPED: it contributes no counts and records why, because a missing certification is not a pass. A check whose certified capability cannot be queried is FAILED: it contributes no counts and fails the run, because an unreadable venue is not an agreeing venue. The two together are the point of the file -- both had previously collapsed into no findings, which is the one answer a money reader must never give.

Capability state comes from Gate.Registry() rather than from type-asserting venue.Reader. A reader that happens to implement four interfaces would otherwise be treated as certified, so the runner asks the authority that holds the certifications instead of inferring capability from the shape of the object in front of it. The account is supplied explicitly and required by the constructor, after a LIMIT 1 lookup proved non-deterministic.

A repeated difference reuses its unresolved case and escalates it in place, and case, audit.record and ops.outbox commit in one transaction. One difference is one case because case_open_material_idx is the index an operator uses to find the blocking break, and one balance disagreement rediscovered every reconciliation interval would otherwise fill it with the same row. Severity comes from the figures with exact decimal arithmetic, and MATERIAL is reserved for a total disagreement or exposure the venue holds and the platform does not, so a one-unit drift on a million does not make MATERIAL meaningless.

Three defects were found by the tests rather than by inspection, and all three are recorded in resolvedGaps: the stored-decimal scan failed for every balance and position because pgx hands NUMERIC back as a string and contracts.Decimal has no Scanner (56); a repeated case could never be written because the outbox sequence was pinned to 1 against a UNIQUE (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, sequence) (57); and keying a balance finding on currency/field opened two cases for one broken currency (58). The first is the one worth remembering, because it failed as FAILED-with-zero-findings with a driver error in the reason -- the exact shape that lets a broken reader look like a healthy one.

15 integration tests in dbtest/reconcile_test.go, all green, against a fake venue.Reader. No concrete adapter exists, so the runner has never read a real venue; that gap is unchanged by this step and is now the only one between this repository and an order that completes end to end.

steps.objective: Close the audit-signing-key hole, because NOT NULL was being read as required
steps.outcome:
This step began as a recorded gap rather than a request, which is how the most consequential finding in this session arrived. The ledger had noted that domain/execution wrote its audit records without SigningKeyID and had deliberately left it alone as too large a change for a proven path. Reading the schema before changing it showed the gap was much larger than one package.

audit.record.signing_key_id is NOT NULL, and NOT NULL is not the same as required -- the empty string satisfies it. The measurement is what makes this a defect rather than a style note: 1298 of 1594 audit records in the test database named no key. That is 81% of the evidence this system produces, and none of it failed, because an empty string that satisfies a constraint looks deliberate.

It had looked harmless because the column comment written in 0006 said it names the key used for the checkpoint that will close the record's batch. Read that way the value is unknowable at append time, so an empty placeholder looked like the honest choice. The premise is false: no migration in this repository issues an UPDATE against that column, and audit.record is append-only besides, so whatever is written at append time is what the record keeps for the life of the partition. The comment is itself the defect, and 0023 corrects it.

domain/ledger had already reached the opposite conclusion and refused an empty key in NewPoster, with a comment explaining exactly this. The OMS and reconciliation paths had not. That is the S22 shape again -- a control one path has and another silently does not -- and it is why the fix went to the schema rather than stopping at the constructors. Two careful constructors do not close a hole that a fourth producer could reopen, so 0023 adds CHECK (length(btrim(signing_key_id)) > 0) NOT VALID, which enforces every new row and tolerates the 1294 that violate it.

The 1294 are not backfilled and no migration should backfill them. No key can honestly be attributed to a record written before one was captured, and inventing a value would manufacture the appearance of attestation for events that have none -- a worse defect than the empty column and much harder to find. They are recorded as a permanent known gap instead, because that is the honest description and because filling the column is the tempting, wrong move.

NOT VALID rather than validated is also the migration discipline, not a compromise: 24_ENTERPRISE_RELEASE_STANDARD.md 5 requires EXPAND-only, and a validated CHECK cannot be added while existing rows violate it.

Verified rather than asserted: after a full 947-test run the count of records naming no key was 1298, exactly the count measured before the run. The corrected code added none. Three tests hold it -- the submission record names the configured key, the case record names it, and the database refuses a record naming none. The third earns its keep, because it is the only one that fails when a future producer forgets to check.

steps.objective: Remediate all 11 findings of the independent /review uncommitted pass, and close the two defects that pass then exposed in the verification instruments themselves
steps.outcome:
Eleven findings accepted and fixed, each with a test that fails when the fix is reverted. Four were behavioural: reconciliation severity aggregation compared severity strings with > rather than by rank, so a balance break's recorded severity was whichever field happened to be compared last and a MATERIAL break could be recorded as MEDIUM (fixed by severityOrder, pinned by TestABalanceCaseRecordsItsWorstFieldNotItsLastOne, which reports severity=MEDIUM and MaterialBreaks=0 under the old comparison); checkOrders read the entire undetermined-order backlog with no bound, so a growing backlog made every reconciliation pass slower without ever reporting incompleteness (defaultMaxOrderProbes=500, WithMaxOrderProbes, LIMIT n+1 so truncation is detectable, and Skipped reporting; three mutations caught); audit.Appender.Append opened and committed its own transaction, so a command using it would commit an audit record for a mutation that then rolled back, which an append-only chain can never withdraw (AppendIn added, five production call sites moved to it, proven by mutating AppendIn to delegate to Append and watching TestAFailedStepRollsBackEveryEarlierWrite fail with 'audit records left behind = 1, want 0'); and the risk gate's external-fact fail-open, closed earlier in the session.

Four were integrity of the mutation instruments: the ledger row was written OUTSIDE the migration transaction, so a failed migration left a ledger entry claiming success (now inside it, proven by an atomicity probe that leaves 0 rows and 0 schema change); applied_at_ns and duration_ms were placeholders rather than measurements (now DB clock_timestamp() and psql \gset, and all 27 rows carry a real epoch nanosecond timestamp and a non-zero duration); the five db/mutate_00*.ps1 scripts could run against any database, took no -Database, and had no guaranteed restore, so an operator could have pointed one at a database they cared about (now restricted to aitc-pg17/aitc, threaded with -Database, and wrapped in try/finally); and dead symbols WithProducer, AdapterIDs, ErrNoDeclaration and ErrAttemptRecordNotDurable were removed.

Three were drift between a Go closed set and the PostgreSQL enum it claims to mirror, all of the same shape: contracts.OrderTypes, contracts.TimeInForces and venue.CertificationStates are now the single enumerators that Valid() and the parity tests both read, so a value added to one side alone fails rather than being silently accepted. Dropping Revoked from the certification states and making order-type or time-in-force validation accept anything are each caught.

Then the instruments failed while proving themselves, which is the part worth keeping. db/verify-schema-live.ps1 read each migration file with two passes -- all CREATE TRIGGERs, then all DROP TRIGGERs -- so migration 0026, which drops and recreates its own trigger in one file to make its no-transaction migration re-runnable, was recorded as declaring and then dropping a trigger, and the gate reported a trigger as MISSING from a database that had it. Fixed by walking statements in file order. And 0027's own RAISE EXCEPTION message contained the words CREATE INDEX inside a string literal, which the gate's non-literal-aware index regex counted as a second declared index, firing PARSE_INCOMPLETE forever against a correct repository; the message is now phrased around the index name.

The trigger dimension had never been fired at anything, which is the same defect the index and constraint dimensions were written to eliminate. T1-T5 now cover dropped, repointed, disabled and undeclared triggers plus a negative control, and the harness is at 17 of 17 assertions with every restore byte-identical. Writing them found two more instrument defects: a trigger is not a regclass, so the schema.table.trigger::regclass shape Get-IndexDef uses returned nothing and the harness restored nothing, leaving the live database one trigger short -- which the gate itself reported as MISSING_TRIGGER, the detector working correctly on a schema the harness had broken; and a mutation whose SQL fails to apply threw out of the whole harness part-way through T2 rather than being recorded as not-detected.

mutationTests.reviewRemediation: 3/3 for the risk-reducing eligibility fix, proven by mutation. domain/risk/evaluate.go evaluateEligibility returned Passed=true for a RiskReducing order BEFORE evaluating the external fact, so it reported 'the external fact is satisfied' for a fact it never checked. The allowlist exemption now covers only the policy half. Two tests pin it: TestRiskReducingActionsStillRequireAReachableVenue fails with 'a risk-reducing action was approved against an unreachable venue' when the evaluateNonLimit call is deleted, and TestRiskReducingActionOnAReachableVenueStillPasses proves the exemption still permits a reachable venue, so the fix cannot be trivially inverted into refusing every reduction.
mutationTests.contracts.Div: 4/4. Reverting Div to a*10^guard/b is caught by contracts TestDivStatesTheQuotientLiterally, TestDivOfAWholeMultipleIsTheExactInteger, domain/instrument TestPreciseNamesTheFirstUnmetBound, and domain/riskstate TestDrawdownStatesTheRatioLiterally, TestConcentrationStatesTheShareLiterally. It is NOT caught by dbtest: the integration fixture's operands share a scale, so the whole database suite stays green with the ratio arithmetic broken.
mutationTests.riskstate.instrumentWiring: 7/7. Discarding instrument.Evaluate's result instead of writing it into OrderFacts is caught by TestAnInstrumentThatPermitsTheOrderIsEligibleAndPrecise, TestASellIsRefusedByAnInstrumentThatCannotBeShorted, TestAnAbsentSideIsRefusedRatherThanReadAsABuy, TestACallerCannotOverrideTheCatalogue, TestAQuantityOffTheInstrumentsGridIsRefused, and by the two pre-existing core gate tests TestTheRiskGateApprovesAnOrderFromARealPolicyRow and TestARiskReducingActionPassesWithNoPolicy.
mutationTests.gate.halts: 2/2, and the first attempt was itself a finding. Short-circuiting the early halt return (`if false && haltDecision.Blocked`) left the whole dbtest suite GREEN: the post-load recheck evaluates the halts a second time and refuses independently, so the early return is an optimization rather than the only enforcement. The meaningful mutant disables both enforcement points and is caught by TestAnActiveHaltRefusesAnOrderTheLimitsWouldPermit, which then reports that the first failed control is VENUE_AVAILABILITY rather than KILL_AND_HALT_STATE and that the refusal no longer names the halt that blocked it.
mutationTests.riskstate.notional: not separately mutated; covered by TestTheComposedGateDeniesOnFactsNothingCanYetSource, which fails if the derived notional is nil or is not 5000.
mutationTests.doc04.enumeration: 2/2. Commenting CtrlLossLimit out of risk.go's `controls` slice fails TestTheControlsAreDoc04sListInDoc04sOrder with 'doc 04 names 15 mandatory checks but the gate implements 14'. Deleting LevelMarket from domain/halt's `levels` fails TestTheHaltPrecedenceMatchesDoc04sChain, which reports doc 04's chain beside the implemented order. Both mutants are caught by the new tests as well as by pre-existing ones.
mutationTests.oms.vocabularies: 2/2. Dropping order_type_not_a_time_in_force from the live schema fails TestIocAndFokBelongToTimeInForceAndOrderTypeForbidsThem. Adding "ICEBERG" to contracts.OrderType.Valid() fails TestContractsOrderTypeCoversEveryValueTheDatabaseHolds ('is true for a value that is not in common.order_type') and, independently, the pre-existing gate test TestAClosedSetIsRefusedByName -- which is the point: the parity test and the behavioural test fail for the same reason from opposite directions.
mutationTests.riskReducing.singleDefinition: Deleting oms.OrderType is compile-time evidence rather than a runtime mutant: removing the type and its RiskReducing method breaks every reference, including the parity test that used to be its only consumer. THE REPLACEMENT FOUND TWO REAL DEFECTS, BOTH IN CODE WRITTEN THIS SESSION, BOTH NOW FIXED.

1. THE TRIGGER GATE WAS BLIND TO AN UNDECLARED TRIGGER WHOSE NAME COLLIDED WITH A DECLARED ONE. The live trigger map was keyed by trigger NAME alone, with last-write-wins, while PostgreSQL makes a trigger name unique per TABLE rather than per schema. Because the query is ordered by table, a second live trigger on a different table was written first and then silently overwritten by the declared one. Measured, on a database that is otherwise exactly correct: creating an undeclared trigger on oms.fill named oms_order_state_machine, alongside the real and correctly placed one on oms.order, produced exit 0 and no finding at all. The gate reported drift=0 while the database carried an extra, unreviewed guard. The map is now keyed by table AND name, a name present on more than one table is reported with the actual tables named, and a live trigger whose table does not match its declaration is reported as UNDECLARED_TRIGGER even when the name is a declared one. Re-proven after the fix: that exact case now exits 1 naming oms.fill and noting that it shares a name with a declared trigger on another table.

Its deliberate SCOPE_UNKNOWN branch was unreachable in practice, because under ErrorActionPreference Stop a native command writing to stderr has its output converted to an ErrorRecord by the stream merge, and the script died on that record before the exit-code check could run. Measured: run from a directory whose module matches no packages, the gate exited 1 with an opaque native-command error and never printed the explanation written for that case. Failing closed by accident of PowerShell's native-command handling is not good enough for a gate, because it means the behaviour depends on an implementation detail rather than on a decision recorded here. The error-action preference is now lowered around the go list call, the exit code is what decides, and the go list diagnostic is quoted in the failure message. A COMMENT THAT MENTIONS DDL WAS SILENTLY CORRUPTING THE COUNTS, AND THE FIRST FIX FOR IT MADE THINGS WORSE. db/migrations/0026 mentions CREATE INDEX three times but declares one index; the other two occurrences are inside comments. On raw text an index section would declare 87, parse 85, and either fail closed forever against a correct repository or report two phantom indexes as missing. So migration text is now read through a lexical comment stripper.

The first stripper was wrong in a way only measurement caught. It tokenised the dollar-quote TAGS ($tag$ and $$) but did not consume the body between them, so the scanner resumed immediately after each opening tag and treated double-hyphen lines INSIDE a dollar-quoted body as comments to blank. A function body is a dollar-quoted string whose CONTENTS are SQL, so those lines are real comments in the database and are stored verbatim in pg_proc.prosrc; blanking them changed the body and produced 31 phantom LIVE_DRIFT reports against a database that was entirely correct. The gate was run before and after the change precisely to notice this, and did. The fix consumes the ENTIRE dollar-quoted region as one token, closing on a backreference to the opening tag, so the scanner resumes after the closing delimiter and can never see a double-hyphen inside a body as a comment. Verified rather than assumed: stripping changes zero of the 66 parsed function bodies, byte-identical hashes before and after, while reducing 0026 CREATE INDEX mentions from 3 to 1. Comments inside a body are deliberately left untouched, because prosrc contains them and therefore the body must.

WHAT THE INDEX DIMENSION DELIBERATELY DOES NOT COMPARE, and why. Comparing declared text against pg_get_indexdef produces false drift on a correct database 38 times over, measured rather than assumed: per-column pg_get_indexdef(idx, colno, true) omits DESC and NULLS FIRST/LAST entirely, so 25 of 84 column lists compared unequal; an IN list deparses to = ANY (ARRAY[...]) with enum type labels attached, so 13 of 30 predicates compared unequal; and the parser adds explicit parentheses around single expressions. A gate that reports 38 phantom differences on a correct schema is worse than no gate, because its green result stops being believed. Key COUNT is compared for all 84 and measured 0 mismatches; column NAMES for the 82 whose declared keys are bare identifiers, also 0 mismatches. That catches the realistic failure, an index rebuilt on the wrong columns, without pretending to a SQL parser. Sort direction and predicates stay an acknowledged gap, printed on every run.

THE INDEX ACCOUNTING REQUIRED EXCLUDING THREE POPULATION SOURCES, each measured, none of them drift: 96 constraint-backed indexes (PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints declared inside CREATE TABLE/ALTER TABLE, which no CREATE INDEX declares, excluded via pg_constraint.conindid); 105 indexes on partition children (automatic replicas of a parent index, the same consequence as the replicated triggers, excluded via relispartition); and index names are unique per SCHEMA, not globally. Measured: state_transition_rule_pkey exists in both oms and strategy. Keying by name alone would silently overwrite the collision and under-report, which is the identical defect the trigger map already paid for once.

MUTATION PROOF, 7 of 7 detected, every restore verified byte-identical, schema green afterwards. The proof is a durable script, db/verify-schema-live-mutations.ps1, because a gate that has only ever been run against a correct schema has been shown to do nothing at all: it would report drift=0 just as happily against a database with every index dropped. Dropped gives MISSING_INDEX (compared_indexes falls to 83). Repointed to another table in the same schema gives INDEX_DRIFT on the table field naming expected and actual. A UNIQUE index silently rebuilt as non-unique gives INDEX_DRIFT on the uniqueness field, the highest-consequence case, because nothing errors and duplicate rows simply become acceptable. Rebuilt on wrong columns gives INDEX_DRIFT on BOTH key count and columns. Left indisvalid=false, the residue of a failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, gives INDEX_INVALID, reported separately because the index exists and is correctly named while the planner ignores it. An undeclared index added live gives UNDECLARED_INDEX. An unparseable CREATE INDEX gives PARSE_INCOMPLETE in an isolated sandbox tree, declared=2 parsed=1 exit 1, which also re-proves the stripper from the other direction, since the fixture comment mention must not be counted or the declared total would be 3.

THE HARNESS CAUGHT A REAL DEFECT IN THE GATE IT WAS TESTING. The undeclared-index probe first came back NOT DETECTED, and the cause was not the detector: the gate counted the undeclared index correctly and printed the finding, but the reporting line read $_.Name on objects whose property is Index, so it printed "ops. on ops.outbox" with the name missing. An accusation that does not name what it accuses is close to useless, and the gate was one step from being declared proven with unreadable index output. Fixed and re-proven.

THE RESTORE PATH FAILED TWICE AGAINST THE LIVE DATABASE BEFORE IT WAS MADE SAFE, and both failures are the kind that hide. A mutation that repoints an index to another table in the same schema leaves the NAME OCCUPIED, so re-creating the captured definition failed with relation already exists and the restore silently did nothing, leaving identity.session_revocation_idx living on role_binding. And DROP INDEX IF EXISTS writes a NOTICE to stderr, which under ErrorActionPreference Stop Windows PowerShell promotes to a terminating NativeCommandError even though psql exited 0; that abort landed INSIDE a finally block, and a throw inside a finally ABORTS the statements after it, so the actual re-creation was skipped and the schema was left mutated. Both times the database was repaired and re-verified. Every restore step is now individually guarded, wrappers judge by exit code rather than by stderr, and the script refuses to report success unless the gate and db/migrate.ps1 are both green at the end.

SCOPE CORRECTED IN THE FILE HEADER in the same change, because it became false the moment the dimension landed. It read that the gate covers function bodies and triggers and does NOT cover constraints, indexes, columns, enums or tables. It now lists the remaining gaps explicitly, including that removing a constraint also removes the only trace of it from this gate view, because constraint-backed indexes are deliberately excluded.
verified.nonAsciiEncodingDefect:
SILENT CHARACTER-LEVEL CORRUPTION, FOUND BY THE NEW GATE. Three functions from db/migrations/0017_configuration_boundary_enforcement.sql were live with '?' where the file has a section sign (U+00A7): config.guard_promotion_provenance, config.guard_revision_mutation and config.assert_no_embedded_secrets. All three now match the repository and the gate reports drift=0 across 64 functions.

Cause, measured two ways. PowerShell 5.1 encodes a native-command pipeline with $OutputEncoding, NOT with [Console]::OutputEncoding, and $OutputEncoding defaults to ASCII. Measured on this host by piping a section sign through psql and reading ascii() back: $OutputEncoding ASCII gives 63 ('?'), $OutputEncoding UTF-8 gives 167. An earlier attempt at this fix set only [Console]::OutputEncoding and changed nothing, because that variable governs console display rather than what is handed to psql.

There were TWO independent defects on the path. The output side above. The input side: in PowerShell 5.1 Get-Content -Raw decodes with the ANSI code page rather than UTF-8, so the section sign arrives as U+00C2 (mojibake) before the pipeline runs. Fixing only $OutputEncoding would have applied a different wrong value, which the live-schema gate would still have reported as drift. db/migrate.ps1 now reads every migration with [System.IO.File]::ReadAllText and sets $OutputEncoding to a BOM-less UTF-8, restoring both encodings on every exit path including the error exits -- an earlier trap-based restore fired on terminating errors but not on exit, leaking the encoding change to any caller that ran the script in-process.

The corruption was invisible to migrate.ps1 by construction: it digests the file on disk, which was correct, while the database held something else. Only functions whose bodies contain a non-ASCII character were affected, which is why 61 of 64 functions matched and the defect survived a migration run that reported no drift. Scope of the harm was cosmetic -- it altered the wording of three error messages, not any control, comparison or condition.
verified.outboxPairingInvariant:
Doc 05 requires that an order committed in SUBMITTING have a durable ops.outbox row. Migration 0024 added the DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED constraint trigger oms_order_submitting_requires_outbox; deferral is required because Command.Prepare writes the order row and the outbox row in one transaction in that order, so an immediate trigger would refuse every correct submission. 0025 replaced the trigger function to match on the canonical order id alone rather than on (aggregate_type, aggregate_id), because aggregate_type is unconstrained free text that this repository writes as both 'ORDER' and 'order'.

MIGRATION 0026 CLOSES A HOLE 0024 LEFT, AND THE HOLE WAS REACHABLE BY A STATEMENT ALREADY IN THIS REPOSITORY. The 0024 trigger is on oms.'order'; it fires when an order ENTERS SUBMITTING and never fires when a row is removed from ops.outbox. So an order could be committed in SUBMITTING, have its outbox row deleted by a later transaction, and -- because every subsequent update leaves the state unchanged and returns early from the guard -- never be checked again. The end state is exactly what 0024 exists to forbid. 0024 justified itself by asserting 'ops.outbox rows are never deleted -- nothing in this repository or its migrations issues a DELETE against them'; that assertion was false, dbtest/dispatch_test.go issued exactly that DELETE.

0026 adds a BEFORE DELETE trigger on ops.outbox that refuses to remove a row naming an order still in SUBMITTING. It is deliberately narrow: the event log remains prunable for everything else, and making ops.outbox append-only would have been the wrong fix for this defect. It identifies orders with common.is_canonical_id(aggregate_id, 'ord'), reusing the schema's own definition rather than a prefix literal -- a literal would also have been wrong, since canonical ids join the prefix with an underscore, making it 'ord_' not 'ord-'. Both halves are tested: TestTheOutboxRowOfASubmittingOrderCannotBeDeleted and TestAnOutboxRowIsPrunableOnceItsOrderHasLeftSubmitting, the second proving the guard is not simply 'never delete'.

Adding the guard broke 10 dispatch tests, which is the correct outcome and worth recording: dbtest/dispatch_test.go cleaned its queue with an unconditional DELETE FROM ops.outbox, and because every test in that file COMMITS a real Prepare, later tests were deleting rows belonging to orders earlier tests had left in SUBMITTING. The cleanup was narrowed to rows not naming a SUBMITTING order rather than the invariant being loosened, and the residue that made a later DispatchOnce count one row too many is retired by retireSubmittedOrder, which drives the order through oms.state_transition_rule (SUBMITTING -> REJECTED is legal only via REJECTED_BY_VENUE) and then prunes.

0026 also adds outbox_aggregate_id_idx, because 0025's change left 0024's index justification stale: outbox_aggregate_sequence_unique leads with (aggregate_type, aggregate_id) and can no longer serve an aggregate_id-only predicate. Verified with enable_seqscan=off, which yields 'Index Only Scan using outbox_aggregate_id_idx, Index Cond: (aggregate_id = ...)'. With the table at 6 rows the planner still prefers a sequential scan, which is correct behaviour and not evidence the index is unused.

A KNOWN WEAKENING, RECORDED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: the guard proves that SOME outbox row names the order, not that a send-owed row exists for it. An unrelated event keyed by the order id would discharge the obligation. Matching on event_type instead would reintroduce exactly the unpinned-literal fragility 0025 removed, and ops.outbox.aggregate_id carries no canonical-id CHECK, so the prefix-uniqueness the guard relies on is an application convention rather than a constraint. The production write path is verified correct -- domain/execution sets AggregateID to the order id and writes ORDER_SUBMIT_REQUESTED -- so this is a latent weakening rather than a live exploit.
verified.migrationReRunnability:
MEASURED AND FIXED 2026-10-03. Appending a documentation comment to 0019 left the live schema correct and left db/migrate.ps1 reporting drift=1, because the ledger records the digest of the bytes that were applied and a comment is still a byte change. Both tempting repairs are wrong. Re-recording the digest is the one repair that must never be chosen, because it makes the edit permanently undetectable while the schema was never rebuilt from it. Re-applying the file as written fails, because CREATE TRIGGER and ADD CONSTRAINT against an existing name are hard errors: 0019 creates three triggers and two CHECK constraints, so it was not re-runnable at all. The fix was mechanical rather than clever: precede each of those five creations with DROP ... IF EXISTS in the same file. 0019 is transactional, so a failed re-apply would have rolled back whole and left nothing behind, which is what made the bounded-failure retry safe to attempt at all. Re-applied in 2293 ms of real work, and a second run reported applied_now=0, so re-runnability is demonstrated rather than asserted. The applied digest is now 80a3c3818e8fe4cff6e402fa3529022d5.

The finding that reaches past 0019: 34 object creations across the migration set have no preceding drop, so most applied migrations in this repository are not re-runnable as written and the identical trap waits in each of them. A lint is the wrong instrument today because it would fire 34 times, and fixing all 34 is a larger change than this warrants. The proportionate action is that db/migrate.ps1 now prints the recovery procedure whenever it reports DRIFT, including the repair that must not be chosen, because a detector that finds a fault but leaves the repair to improvisation converts a detected fault into an unrecoverable one.

It confirmed there is no crash-as-pass path: the harness has no top-level try/catch, so an unhandled terminating error exits non-zero before exit 0, and the tally requires zero failures AND a green gate AND a green migrate.
