It found three defects, all in the EVIDENCE RECORD rather than the harness code, and all three are fixed: a blanket claim in docs/26 that a restore is verified by hex 'never by comparing strings' when only the function dimension does that (the index, constraint and trigger dimensions still compare deparsed strings, at verify-schema-live-mutations.ps1:189, :379, :495), an unreconcilable '9 of 9' tally written into this file, and a misattribution that put F2's dollar sign in the function body when it is in the signature (p_path TEXT DEFAULT '$', db/migrations/0017:144). Two LOW items in the harness were also fixed on its advice: F4's '-lt 3' also admitted parsed=0, which a gate whose function pattern matched nothing would produce, so the count is now pinned to exactly 2; and '$hexAfter -eq $hexBefore' would treat '$null -eq $null' as byte-identical, so an unreadable body now fails explicitly instead of reading as a pass. One reviewer claim was itself wrong and was not adopted: it stated that 73 of 74 bodies begin with a newline, but the measured figures are 55 of 63 beginning and 63 of 63 ending, so the documentation was corrected to the measured numbers rather than to the reviewer's.
verified.fullSuiteReverifiedAfterDatabaseRebuild: FULL GO SUITE RE-VERIFIED 2026-10-03 AGAINST A REBUILT DATABASE. This closes the one gap left open at the end of the function-dimension work. The database in this repository is not a given: that work had to DROP and rebuild it from the migration files, because the harness had left two functions drifted and the correct repair was to rebuild rather than hand-patch. The 955 tests in verified.testsTotal run against that live database, so every test claim in this file had silently become a claim about a database that no longer existed. docs/26 already says the rule -- 'use -count=1 after any change to the database or to a migration, because a cached pass cannot verify a post-restore state' -- and a rebuild is the largest possible such change. Measured after the rebuild: 'go test -v ./... -count=1 -p 1' with AITC_TEST_DATABASE_URL set and packages run serially, exit 0. 955 pass / 0 fail / 0 skip = 589 top-level + 366 subtests across 14 tested packages, with services/audit and services/reconcile still reporting no test files. Every figure already recorded here reconciles, not only the total: dbtest 359+66=425, the domain aggregate 145+172=317, and contracts+adapters/venue+services/dispatch 85+128=213, plus the individual package keys testsContracts=170, testsAdaptersVenue=21 and testsServicesDispatch=22. The method is the one in verified.testCountingMethod, unchanged. Also re-verified in the same state and unchanged: db/verify-gofmt.ps1 reports packages=16 go_files_examined=88 unformatted=0, and go vet ./... is clean. The 955 tests left no residue -- the schema gate still reports drift=0 across 64 functions, 27 triggers, 85 indexes and 262 constraints, and db/migrate.ps1 still reports applied_now=0 failures=0 drift=0.

G1.scopeLimit: Domain Foundation only. Nothing can place an order: no repository, OMS orchestrator, ledger poster, reconciliation executor, identity service or configuration service exists. The four domain packages are pure logic with no database access.
G1.note: PASS recorded 2026-09-30T11:20Z. Was FAIL until two criteria were closed by real code: 0020 (canonical ID parity) and the domain packages with 78 unit + 6 parity tests.

G2.note: 16a/16b/16d closed by 0019, each with live-database tests, and the findings document now records what each became rather than only what it found. 16c (feed freshness) is deliberately NOT closed, and measurement on 2026-10-03 established that it is downstream of a missing component rather than pending on a decision alone: market.feed_health has no maintainer (0 Go references outside dbtest, 0 rows, its only trigger computes nothing), so a partial fix reading health_state would be vacuously true on absent data -- strictly worse than the unconditional denial it replaces -- or vacuously false, pointing an operator at an empty table. The chain is concrete venue adapter -> feed health writer -> 16c -> MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL's reference price, which makes the G2 and G3 blockers the same item. The scope question (market_class alone, +venue_id, +instrument_id -- not refinements of one another) is still required and is now the SECOND thing to settle rather than the first. CONSEQUENCE: market.feed_health and market.freshness_policy currently record observations that no risk path reads, so an operator watching a DEGRADED feed may reasonably conclude trading is blocked when it is not. See the OPEN QUESTION section at the end of 0019 and Remediation outcome in the findings document.

G3.note:
The risk gate is composed and the OMS submit/resolve lifecycle is fully durable. domain/gate is the single entry point for a risk decision. domain/execution has exactly two commands, Command.Prepare and Command.Resolve, both of which write the OMS journal, the submission record, an audit record and an outbox row in one transaction, and both of which are proven against the live tables. The superseded in-memory Submitter has been deleted, so there is one door to each operation and no path that mutates an order without a durable record. Ledger posting, the dispatcher and reconciliation execution all exist now -- the ledger poster commits balanced postings and refuses a duplicate, services/dispatch reads ops.outbox, and services/reconcile executes the four checks with no silent-clean outcome.

What remains is one thing, and measurement on 2026-10-03 established that G3 and G2 are blocked by the SAME item rather than by two. A concrete venue adapter. Everything upstream of the send site runs against the live PostgreSQL schema, but the send site and the reconciliation reader both terminate in a test double, so no real venue can be certified, nothing can be sent, and nothing has ever been reconciled against a real venue. Downstream of the adapter sit, in order: a feed health writer (market.feed_health is measured to have no maintainer and zero rows, so 16c cannot even be partially implemented), the 16c freshness control itself, and the sourced reference price MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL needs before it can evaluate a market order. Building any of those three against a fake adapter would be inventing the last mile rather than implementing it. Live trading remains blocked; G11 is not in scope.

G11.note: live activation; not to be attempted

nextObjective.name: G3 - Trading Core
preconditions: domain/gate is the composed entry point and is the only supported way to reach a risk decision: it accepts order terms, derives the risk-reducing predicate itself, reads policy and halts from committed rows, and takes transactional account, position, strategy and instrument state through riskstate.Querier. Everything below it is tested in isolation and none of it is a supported caller.

Go/SQL parity is enforced by dbtest/domain_parity_test.go and dbtest/risk_policy_parity_test.go, which read the live tables and information_schema. risk.ProjectedColumns is the single source of truth for the Go side, so a column added to risk.policy without being projected fails the test.

Doc 04 is now a test input, not only a comment. domain/risk/doc04_test.go and domain/halt/doc04_test.go read the document and assert the gate's 15 controls and the halt hierarchy against it, in both directions and in order. Editing doc 04 without editing the gate -- or the reverse -- fails the build.

The gate denies on facts it cannot source: VENUE_AVAILABILITY, MARKET_DATA_FRESHNESS and DUPLICATE_ORDER_DETECTION have no table in this repository. That is a fail-closed design, not a defect, and the composition tests assert the denial names exactly those three.

max_order_quantity and max_price_deviation are projected onto Policy but read by no control, because doc 04 names neither. Awaiting an owner decision: add controls, or confirm the columns are vestigial.

MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL now derives the order's notional from its own quantity and price, and denies a market order because no price exists at submission. Closing that needs a sourced reference price (G2 16c).
Live trading stays disabled; G11 is BLOCKED and is not in scope.

The canonical identifier prefixes the schema demands and the prefixes Go can mint are now compared in both directions by dbtest/canonical_id_prefix_parity_test.go, reading pg_constraint from the live catalog. Twelve prefixes the schema already required were absent from contracts.EntityTypes() (act, bal, ckp, dep, edl, jnl, oe1, rck, sbm, sys, trn, wid), so no Go code could mint a value for execution.submission.submission_id or eleven other columns. The pre-existing encoder parity test could not see it because common.canonical_id_from_bytes takes its prefix as TEXT and formats whatever it is given, so both encoders agreed about all 29 prefixes Go had

The durable submission record is implemented in domain/execution/store.go against execution.submission. The Go and database outcome vocabularies have different cardinalities and non-corresponding names (ACCEPTED stores as ACKNOWLEDGED, UNDETERMINED as TIMED_OUT_UNKNOWN, and PENDING, FILLED and CANCELLED exist only in the database), so the mapping is pinned in both directions against the live CHECK constraint rather than against a Go constant. Every unrecognised Go outcome stores as TIMED_OUT_UNKNOWN and every unrecognised stored value refuses the read; both defaults are deliberate, because the opposite choice -- REJECTED -- would durably assert that no exposure exists on the strength of a value the platform does not understand. Seven integration tests against the live table, with four mutation proofs: REJECTED stored as PENDING, an uninterpretable stored value defaulting to REJECTED, PENDING read as ACCEPTED, and an uninterpretable stored row skipped

Venue certification is now load-bearing, at two call sites that are deliberately not the same check. domain/execution.Command.Prepare refuses before opening a transaction, and NewCommand refuses a nil SubmissionGate so no construction path yields a Command that can prepare an order without a certification authority behind it. adapters/venue.SubmitPublisher.Publish re-checks immediately before the venue call, because a certificate valid at Prepare can be withdrawn during the commit, claim and lease that separate preparation from the send. SubmitIntent.AdapterID is a required field for the same reason a nil gate is refused: a submission that does not name its adapter has no certification to look up

Reconciliation execution now exists (services/reconcile, S24). The four checks doc 05 names are implemented and each is COMPLETED, SKIPPED or FAILED; an uncertified capability is skipped with a reason and a certified-but-unqueryable one fails the run, so neither can masquerade as a clean venue. 15 integration tests are green. The order probe is deliberately narrow -- only orders whose outcome is unestablished -- and an unmappable venue state is reported rather than guessed

A concrete venue adapter does not exist, and it is now the last thing between this repository and an order that could actually complete. Everything upstream of it -- gate, prepare, dispatch, ledger, audit, outbox, send site and reconciliation -- runs against the live PostgreSQL schema. The send path and the reconciliation reader both terminate in a double, so no real venue can be certified and nothing reconciles a real venue
nextObjective.rationale:
G1 is closed. The risk gate is composed and sources every fact it measures. OMS submission and resolution are durable, the dispatcher turns committed outbox rows into publisher calls, the ledger poster commits balanced postings and refuses a duplicate, venue certification is enforced both before an order is prepared and again before it is sent, and reconciliation now executes against the live tables. What G3 still requires is a concrete venue adapter, and the 2026-10-03 measurement established that this single item also blocks G2 16c, a feed health writer and MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL's reference price, because all of them need something that observes a real feed. Until one exists nothing can be certified, so nothing can be sent, the reconciliation reader has nothing real to read, and there is no data source for a freshness control to read. The adapter is the next objective because it is the only remaining gap, and because a submission that can become UNKNOWN is only safe if something resolves it, which now exists but has never seen a real venue.

It is also the one gap that cannot be closed by writing more Go. Every component in this repository upstream of the send site is tested against the live schema and behaves as specified; the missing piece needs a real venue, real credentials and a real endpoint, none of which this environment has. Inventing an adapter against a fake venue would produce the appearance of the last mile while leaving every downstream control reading a double -- the same failure as shipping a guessed freshness scope rule, and for the same reason.

knownGaps: SUPERSEDED 2026-10-02, retained so the correction is not silently rewritten: services/reconcile checkBalances was recorded above as possibly carrying the same per-row query shape as checkFills and checkPositions, and as unaudited. It was then audited and it DID: reconcile.go issued one QueryRowContext per currency at the old line 779. All three reconciliation checks now read in one grouped query each, so this gap is closed rather than carried. The reason it survived the original review is the reason it is worth keeping: two of a kind is a pattern, and a review that fixes the two it found has not thereby checked the third

The three 0017 config.* functions whose bodies contain section signs were re-applied by hand during the reset investigation. The encoding path itself was MEASURED correct (ascii('section sign')=167 through the exact pipeline migrate.ps1 uses, and a plpgsql function created through that pipeline stored the character intact), so this was stale database state rather than a transport defect -- but the provenance of that stale state is not established, and a clean container built from scratch should be checked once to confirm it does not recur

audit.record.occurred_at_ns_bound and recorded_at_ns_bound are declared NOT VALID by migration 0021. Historical rows are therefore uncertified; nothing validates them in-band. The VALIDATE CONSTRAINT statements are recorded in the migration but are not scheduled or automated

domain/execution has no production caller. The durable submission record is now implemented (domain/execution/store.go) and proven against the live table, but nothing in a running path calls RecordAttempt before a send or reads History to build the attempt history, so the invariant is still not load-bearing outside tests

SubmissionRequest.PreviousAttempts is still supplied by the caller rather than by execution.Store.History. The store can now supply it -- History reads the durable rows and UndeterminedDurable refuses rather than reporting none -- but Submit has not been wired to it, so the caller can still assemble an empty slice and omit a row. This is the last seam between the no-retry invariant and durable state

The transaction boundary for a submit is NOT an open owner decision. Doc 05 'Transaction boundary' settles it: domain validation, state mutation, audit record creation and outbox insertion execute in one PostgreSQL transaction, and the dispatcher is a separate reader using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. An earlier note here called this an open design question; that was wrong and the doc governs it. The durable PENDING submission row belongs inside that transaction, and the venue call happens after it commits

The OMS state machine has no UNKNOWN -> SUBMITTING rule, so attempts > 1 for one order_id is unreachable through legal transitions and submission_retry_requires_reconciliation is defence in depth against a machine that already forbids the retry. Whether that is intended or whether a recovery-path transition is missing is a specification question for the owner; the tests reach the rule by seeding a submission row directly rather than by manufacturing an illegal transition

doc 05 states that a committed state mutation always has a corresponding durable outbox record, and NO trigger enforces the pairing -- there is no trigger on oms.order or execution.submission. It holds only because domain/execution.Command.Prepare writes the row, which a mutation proof confirms is load-bearing. A command that forgets it would leave an order SUBMITTING with nothing committed to send it and no system would complain

audit.Appender.Append opens its own transaction and therefore could not satisfy doc 05's requirement that audit record creation join the command's transaction. AppendIn was added for that composition. Without it, a submit would commit audit evidence for a mutation that then rolled back, and the append-only chain cannot withdraw the record afterwards

SUPERSEDED at S24, retained so the earlier claim is not silently rewritten: reconciliation execution did not exist, so an UNKNOWN submission was durable and unattended. It now exists in services/reconcile with 15 green integration tests. What remains true of this gap is narrower: the runner has never read a real venue, because no adapter exists to certify

The composed gate cannot approve anything in this repository today. VENUE_AVAILABILITY, MARKET_DATA_FRESHNESS and DUPLICATE_ORDER_DETECTION have no persisted authority, so every order is refused on 'not established'. This is recorded rather than worked around: the composition tests assert the refusal names exactly those three, so the assertion fails loudly when one becomes sourceable and the remaining gap is smaller than the test claims
A market order is refused by MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL because notional is nil, and the gate would need a sourced reference price to evaluate it. No price feed is consulted anywhere (G2 16c)

domain/instrument reads market.instrument and riskstate.Load now calls instrument.Evaluate for every order, so eligibility and precision validity are sourced rather than asserted, and the caller's values are overwritten. STILL OPEN: venue availability and market data freshness remain caller-supplied booleans because no table in this repository holds them

contracts.Decimal exports Coef() at money.go:201 and go doc reports it, but the compiler does not resolve it -- in-package or cross-package, on a clean build cache, and for a selector on a variable while the same selector on a conversion or composite literal resolves. Every other method on Decimal, including the unexported coeff(), resolves normally. Nothing depends on it: IncrementMultiple now uses Div/Mul. Recorded rather than worked around, because it is a toolchain anomaly that a future reader will otherwise rediscover at cost -- CLOSED, and the finding itself was false. Re-tested directly rather than re-reasoned: a probe package inside the module selecting Coef() on a Decimal VARIABLE, which is the exact case the gap names as failing, compiles and prints 7. Cross-package resolution therefore works, which alone falsifies the cross-package half of the claim. Nothing here required a toolchain anomaly to be explained, so the gap was recording a measurement that did not hold; retained above in its original wording so it is not mistaken for something that was ever true -- see resolvedGaps defect 60

max_order_quantity and max_price_deviation are projected but read by no control. Doc 04's risk gate is exactly 15 bullets and names neither a quantity cap nor a price-deviation cap, and that is now verified against the document rather than believed: domain/risk/doc04_test.go pins the 15, and TestColumnsWithNoDoc04Control pins these two as the only policy columns with no control. Closing the gap means changing doc 04, which is a specification change and therefore an owner decision, not an engineering one

ownerDecision: whether market.instrument.order_types and risk.policy.permitted_order_types should continue listing IOC and FOK. Migration 0022 stops oms.order carrying a time-in-force instruction in its order_type column, so an instrument may still advertise IOC/FOK support and an order expresses it through time_in_force. That is consistent, but it is a distinction a reader has to be told, and doc 16 does not currently say it

SUBMIT_FAILED and CANCEL_REQUESTED are valid event kinds that drive no transition, so a submit that fails before reaching the venue and a cancel that is requested but not yet effected have no move in the machine. Whether that is correct depends on whether the venue adapter reports those as SUBMITTING -> REJECTED via REJECTED_BY_VENUE, which is what the table currently implies
permitted_sides, permitted_order_types and permitted_modes are loaded and deliberately unprojected: no doc 04 control validates them
Invariant 8 is defence in depth only; the primary control is architectural and unimplemented
Halt and operational-mode gates cover the OMS order state machine only
0018 gate reads committed rows; a same-transaction case cannot block an order
audit.verify_checkpoint_signature_crypto does not exist; needs KMS/HSM

MEASURED 2026-10-03, AND IT IS A SEQUENCING FACT RATHER THAN A POLICY QUESTION. 16c was recorded as blocked on an owner decision about which market.freshness_policy row governs an order. That is still required and it is still unanswered, but it is the SECOND thing to settle, and finding that out changed what a partial fix would mean. market.feed_health has no maintainer: 0 Go references to feed_health or freshness_policy anywhere in domain/, services/, adapters/ or contracts/; 0 rows in the table; and the only trigger on it, feed_sequence_monotonic, refuses a backwards watermark and computes nothing. health_state is written by no production statement -- the only writes are two dbtest fixtures inside transactions that roll back.

That rules out the obvious partial fix, which is the reason this is recorded rather than left as a note. Reading health_state without the age bound looks like the safe half of 16c, because every direction it can refuse in is the refusing direction. It reads a column no process maintains over a table that is empty, and an aggregate over that table is one of exactly two things: NOT EXISTS(any feed that is not HEALTHY) is vacuously true and the control PASSES on absent data, which turns a fail-closed control fail-open on its default state; EXISTS(a HEALTHY feed) is vacuously false and every order is denied for a reason naming feed health when the real cause is that nothing feeds the table. The first is strictly worse than today's unconditional denial, because it looks like the defect 0019 exists to catch. The second reproduces the original 16c failure verbatim.

So 16c is downstream of a component that does not exist. The chain is: concrete venue adapter -> feed health writer -> 16c freshness control -> MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL reference price. The last link was already recorded as a dependency; the first two were not, and they are what makes this sequencing rather than scheduling. This also means the G3 blocker and the G2 blocker are the SAME item, which was not previously stated anywhere and is the most useful thing this measurement produced.
0019 16c: feed freshness controls are not consulted anywhere
Doc 17 section 4's separately-defined audited safe-reduction policy does not exist; risk-reducing actions bypass all limits and record that fact rather than checking a cap
The risk gate has only ever run against the paper environment; no live account or venue state has fed it
Gross exposure is marked at average_entry_price because no price feed is consulted; it understates a position whose market price has risen (G2 16c dependency)
MINOR_BREAK reconciliation is excluded from tradeable, so a break judged minor halts trading. That is an owner decision this repository has not recorded

Verification depends on a local Docker container (aitc-pg17 on port 55439). If Docker Desktop is not running, the entire dbtest package fails at connection time and reports ~253 failures that say nothing about the code. The ledger records this so a future reader does not read it as a regression

domain/execution still has no production caller. Command.Prepare and Command.Resolve are both durable and both proven against the live tables, but no dispatcher reads ops.outbox to make the venue call and no reconciliation runner supplies a Resolver, so nothing invokes either command in a running path. This is the remaining seam between the durable lifecycle and the world.

permits resolution by "an authorized recovery procedure"; Resolve enforces that a procedure acted and said who, not that it was authorized. Operational-mode release already requires dual control (G3/G11 scope), so the missing piece is specifically an authorization check on resolution.

services/dispatch now has both kinds of test, but the split is not the one first assumed. The database-independent surface is covered in-package by dispatch_test.go (8 tests, 22 with subtests): truncate, the constructor refusals, both fluent setters, the clock seam and the ErrUnroutable sentinel. What still cannot be tested without PostgreSQL is everything that decides WHICH rows exist and WHEN an attempt is spent -- the batch limit, the lease cutoff, the attempt ceiling, and the claim query itself -- because those live in SQL against ops.outbox. A stub querier was the wrong remedy and was deliberately not built: the ceiling arithmetic is only correct if it agrees with outbox_exhausted_is_dead_lettered and outbox_attempts_bounded, and a stub would agree with whatever the stub was told. Closing this properly means either an injected executor interface or accepting that this package's correctness is a property of Go-and-schema agreement, which is what dbtest/dispatch_test.go actually tests.

The local aitc-pg17 container rejected TCP password auth for the postgres role three times in this session -- 306 failed connections in one run -- and the cause was NOT identified. The role's SCRAM verifier did not match the documented dev password, yet no migration, script or test in the repo issues ALTER ROLE, the container's POSTGRES_PASSWORD matches that password exactly, only one container owns port 55439, and polling pg_authid every 250ms across a full run recorded zero changes. Re-applying the documented password through the local trust socket restored the suite and it has stayed green across three consecutive runs, so this is recorded as unexplained rather than fixed.

One trap is worth naming: docker exec psql authenticates over the local socket against a trust rule and therefore does NOT prove password auth works. The pg_hba trust entries for 127.0.0.1 and ::1 mask exactly the failures a host-side test run hits, which is why the drift first presented as a perfectly healthy database.

risk_gate_integration_test.go and gate_composition_test.go share a second counter, policySeq, which also starts at 0 and also mints ids that some fixtures commit. It happens not to collide today, but it carries the same defect 52 shape and the same file-order dependency. It was left alone deliberately: it is pre-existing, currently green, and fixing it is not needed for the dispatcher. Anyone adding a committing fixture to either file should give it a band of its own rather than extending that counter.

dbtest.UniqueSequence still cannot guarantee uniqueness across two coincidental runs. Two runs whose nonces share a masked multiplier produce identical sequences, roughly once in a hundred thousand runs, because the multiplier is the only input that varies. The sequenceFloor added for defect 53 keeps that collision out of the range other tests hardcode, so it is an ordinary duplicate-key failure inside the two runs concerned and a reset clears it -- but the underlying coincidence is unreached and is not fixed. It is pinned by TestUniqueSequenceCollidesWithAnotherCoincidentalRun so that it is documented rather than assumed absent. Making it genuinely unique would mean taking the run identifier from a source with no birthday collision (a migrated ledger sequence or a supplied value) rather than from a clock.

domain/execution/command.go writes its audit records without SigningKeyID, so audit.record.signing_key_id is being set to the empty string. The column is NOT NULL, which means the schema accepts an unsigned audit record for every order submission and resolution rather than refusing it. This was found while building the ledger poster, which refuses an empty signing key for exactly this reason (NewPoster takes one and rejects ''). The OMS path predates that decision and was not changed, because altering proven, mutation-tested submit and resolve paths is a larger change than the gap warrants on its own. Until it is closed, an OMS audit record is not attributable to a key. -- CLOSED at S25, see resolvedGaps defect 59. Retained above in its original wording so the change is not mistaken for something that was always true.

1294 pre-existing audit records name no signing key and are permanently unattributable (created by defect 59, deliberately NOT closed). audit.record.signing_key_id is '' on these rows, which the 0023 constraint is NOT VALID so it tolerates -- 24_ENTERPRISE_RELEASE_STANDARD.md 5 requires every migration to be EXPAND-only, and a validated CHECK cannot be added while they violate it. They are not backfilled, and no migration should backfill them: there is no key that can be honestly attributed to a record written before one was captured, so inventing a value would manufacture the appearance of attestation for events that have none. That is a worse defect than the empty column and far harder to discover. These records cover order submissions, outcome resolutions and venue answers from before S25. Whether evidence this old ever needs to be defensible is an owner decision; the honest options are to accept the gap explicitly or to let the retention policy expire the partitions, and the dishonest one is to fill the column.

A ledger journal cannot express a two-account transfer. ledger.journal_must_balance resolves the header by (journal_id, account_id, currency) and raises foreign_key_violation when the leg's account or currency does not match, so every leg of a journal must share its header's account and currency. Combined with journal_balanced requiring debits = credits and journal_totals_positive requiring both to be non-zero, a journal is necessarily a set of balanced legs on ONE account, and a single-leg journal is impossible. ledger.entry_kind contains TRANSFER, which cannot be balanced within a single account. This is a schema property, not an implementation gap, and it is recorded here because any future cash-movement design has to know it before it is designed rather than on discovering it in a deferred constraint error.

RESIDUAL of the closed live-drift gap: db/verify-schema-live.ps1 compares FUNCTION BODIES only. Triggers, CHECK and FK constraints, indexes, columns, enums and tables are not compared against the repository, so a trigger dropped from the live database, or a CHECK constraint removed, or an enum value added, is still invisible to every gate in the repository. The original gap was found only because a function body happened to be the thing that was mutated; the same class of divergence in any other object type would not be caught today. Closing this needs the objects re-derived from the migration files the way function bodies now are, and it is deliberately not claimed as done.

MEASURED RESIDUAL, NOT INFERRED. Migration 0026's guard on ops.outbox is a ROW-level trigger, and PostgreSQL does not fire row-level triggers for TRUNCATE. Measured against a real committed order in SUBMITTING with its outbox row present, using a throwaway probe that was deleted after it ran:

    DELETE FROM ops.outbox WHERE event_id = ...  -> REFUSED by the 0026 guard
    DELETE FROM oms."order"     WHERE order_id =  -> REFUSED by FK order_event_order_id_fkey
    TRUNCATE ops.outbox                          -> ALLOWED, and the protected row was destroyed

The first probe of this question was run against an EMPTY table, where all three commands succeed trivially and the result proves nothing; it had to be re-run with real data to be worth anything.

The residual is accepted rather than closed. No code in domain/, services/ or adapters/ issues a TRUNCATE, and it requires the TRUNCATE privilege. dbtest/dbtest.go's Committed helper does issue one, but it truncates ops.outbox together with oms."order" in a single statement, so it removes the order and its record together instead of orphaning an order whose record has gone, which is the state the guard exists to prevent. A BEFORE TRUNCATE trigger that refused unconditionally would break legitimate test infrastructure while preventing nothing for the application's own writes that the DELETE guard does not already prevent. Closing it fully would mean a statement-level trigger plus a redesign of the Committed helper's cleanup, and that is a deliberate deferral rather than an oversight.

MEASURED RESIDUAL IN THE LIVE SCHEMA GATE, not inferred. The index dimension compares existence, schema, table, uniqueness, key count, column names and validity. It deliberately does NOT compare an index predicate (WHERE clause) or its sort direction, and both were measured before being excluded rather than assumed comparable. Comparing declared text against pg_get_indexdef on a database that is entirely correct produced 38 mismatches: per-column pg_get_indexdef omits DESC and NULLS FIRST/LAST, which accounted for 25 of 84 column lists; an IN list deparses to = ANY (ARRAY[...]) with enum type labels, which accounted for 13 of 30 predicates; and the parser adds explicit parentheses around single expressions. A gate that reports 38 phantom differences on a correct schema is worse than no gate, because its green result stops being believed, so key count (all 84, 0 mismatches) and column names (82 of 84, 0 mismatches) were chosen instead. The 2 expression-keyed indexes have their key COUNT compared but not their key EXPRESSIONS. Separately, constraint-backed indexes are excluded from the scan because no CREATE INDEX declares them, which means removing a PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY or CHECK constraint also removes the only trace of it from this gate view. All of these are stated in the script header so the gate cannot be reported as general schema-drift coverage.

RESIDUAL OF THE CONSTRAINT DIMENSION, measured rather than assumed. db/verify-schema-live.ps1 now compares every NAMED table constraint for existence, type and validation state, but three parts of the constraint surface are still invisible to it and none of them is a caveat. First, unnamed constraints are not compared in EITHER direction: the 46 anonymous PRIMARY KEYs and the inline column-level REFERENCES foreign keys, whose names PostgreSQL generates, are neither required nor reported. This direction was implemented and then removed, because it falsely accused oms_order_submitting_requires_outbox and feed_observed_sequence_non_negative, both of which are declared in the migrations; a gate that names constraints the repository declares is worse than one that stays silent. Second, a CHECK expression is not compared, only its existence, type and validation state, because PostgreSQL deparse rewrites the expression and text comparison reports phantom differences on a correct schema, which is the same measured result that ruled out index predicates and sort direction. Third, a FOREIGN KEY referenced table, referenced columns and ON DELETE/ON UPDATE action are not compared. The residual that matters is the combination: a constraint can have its expression weakened, or its referential target repointed to a different table, and the gate stays green, because the constraint still exists under the declared name with the declared type.

RESIDUAL OF THE CONSTRAINT DIMENSION, second half. The declared-constraint parser recognises a constraint only where it can be attributed to a table by the nearest preceding CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE, so it does not parse CREATE TABLE bodies at all. That is a deliberate trade rather than a limitation to be apologised for: a version that did parse bodies was measured before being written up and matched only 49 of the 65 CREATE TABLE statements in this repository, because a closing parenthesis inside a string literal ends the body early and silently truncates the rest, capturing 172 of 251 CHECK constraints with no error raised. Coverage of the shipped version was then verified from the other direction, by cross-checking every live constraint against the declared set: 5 uncovered, all contype=t constraint triggers already covered by the trigger dimension. The two failure modes are not symmetric, which is why the narrow version was kept: under-coverage can still be MEASURED against the live database, whereas a truncation bug is invisible from inside the parser.

MEASURED DEFECT IN THE CONSTRAINT PARSER, found and fixed during this work, recorded because the shape recurs. A newline-blind capture of the constraint body silently dropped 84 of 268 named constraints -- every multi-line CHECK -- while the gate still reported drift=0 and still passed its own parse-completeness check, because those constraints were never counted as declared in the first place. It was caught only by cross-checking against live, not by the parse-completeness check, which is precisely the check everyone would assume covers this case. Letting the capture cross newlines fixed the count but made the gate exceed a 600s budget, so the type keyword is now matched directly in the pattern instead; that is both correct and fast, and it excludes CONSTRAINT TRIGGER for free. Runtime went from over 600s to 39s with the same 262 constraints compared.
resolvedGaps:
An audit record could assert anything while naming no key that attests to it (defect 59). audit.record.signing_key_id is NOT NULL, and NOT NULL is not the same as required: the empty string satisfies it. domain/execution wrote '' on every ORDER_SUBMIT_PREPARED, every ORDER_OUTCOME_RESOLVED and every ORDER_SUBMIT_ANSWERED, and services/reconcile wrote '' on every case opened or escalated. The measurement is the finding: 1298 of 1594 audit records in the test database named no key, so this was 81% of the evidence rather than a theoretical hole. It survived because the empty string looks deliberate, and because the column comment from 0006 said it names 'the key used for the checkpoint that will close this record's batch' -- a value that is unknowable at append time, so '' read as an honest placeholder. It was never a placeholder: no migration anywhere in this repository issues an UPDATE against that column, and audit.record is append-only besides, so whatever is written at append time is what the record keeps for the life of the partition. domain/ledger had already reached the opposite conclusion and refused an empty key in NewPoster; the OMS and reconciliation paths had not, which is the same class of failure as S22 -- a control one path has and another silently does not.

Three changes, and the third is the one that matters. domain/execution takes a signing key and returns ErrNoSigningKey for '', a sibling of ErrNoSubmissionGate because both answer the same question, which is whether there is anything here that can be held to account later. services/reconcile does the same through WithSigningKey. But two careful constructors do not close a hole that three new producers could reopen, so migration 0023 adds CHECK (length(btrim(signing_key_id)) > 0) NOT VALID to audit.record, and corrects the column comment to describe what the column actually holds. Three tests hold it: the submission record names the configured key, the case record names it, and the database refuses a record that names none. The last is the one that earns its keep -- it fails if a future producer forgets to check, which is the case constructors cannot cover.

Verified rather than asserted: after a full 947-test run the count of records naming no key was 1298, exactly the count before the run. The fixed code added none.

The reconciliation runner could not read a single stored decimal (defect 56). pgx returns NUMERIC through database/sql as a string and contracts.Decimal has no sql.Scanner, so every balance and position read failed with 'unsupported Scan, storing driver.Value type string into type *contracts.Decimal'. The failure had the worst possible shape for a reader: the check reported FAILED with a finding count of zero and a reason naming a driver error rather than a missing balance, so a run whose money could not be read was indistinguishable from a run that found nothing wrong. The columns are now selected as ::text and parsed by decimalFrom, which follows the decision already taken for risk.policy's text[] columns -- the read is adapted at the read site rather than teaching a core contract type about a driver. Parsing NUMERIC(38,18) text is exact, which is the reason PostgreSQL does not send it as a float. decimalFrom also refuses a NULL rather than reading it as zero, because a missing balance and an empty one must not compare as agreement.

A repeated difference could never be recorded, so every pass opened a new case (defect 57). ops.outbox carries UNIQUE (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, sequence) and the runner wrote sequence = 1 for every case, so the second record for one case collided and rolled back. The symptom was worse than a crash: the case row, its audit record and its outbox row are written in one transaction, so the collision silently abandoned the evidence refresh of an existing case while the run reported no case error. The outbox sequence is now read as max(sequence)+1 within the transaction, the same shape domain/execution uses for an order's own event sequence. One consequence of case reuse is that a case legitimately has several outbox rows -- one on open, one on escalation, one per evidence refresh -- which is why a fixed sequence could only ever have been correct while cases were never reused.

One disagreeing currency produced two cases (defect 58). The balance finding was keyed on currency/field, so a single missed fill that breaks both total and available opened two rows in case_open_material_idx and two items on the operator's list, while fixing the actual cause closes both. The identity of the difference is the currency; which fields disagree is evidence attached to it, retained in full so the grouping hides nothing. The case records the widest gap and the highest severity across the fields, so a break graded from one field is never understated because another happened to be closer.

A missing account was resolved by LIMIT 1, which made the runner non-deterministic. With several accounts present, a reconciliation could compare one account's balance against the venue's aggregate and report a MATERIAL break that was an artefact of the row the query happened to return. The account is now supplied explicitly through WithAccount and the constructor requires one, so the thing being compared is named rather than inferred.
