and doc 01 invariant 3 require reconciliation or an authorized recovery procedure first, and nothing enforced it: the venue adapter caused the timeout, the risk gate evaluates an order that has not been sent, and a CHECK constraint sees one row rather than the history of how many times it was sent. domain/execution enforces it over an attempt history carried on SubmissionRequest.PreviousAttempts, which is a required field with no default so a caller who omits it gets a compile error instead of a silent resubmission. Resolve is a separate method on a separate interface because resolution is a read of venue state, and conflating it with submission is how a reconciliation becomes an accidental second order.

The orchestrator recorded RISK_APPROVED -> ACKNOWLEDGED as a single move, which the closed set does not permit (defect 46). Doc 04 places SUBMITTING between RISK_APPROVED and every venue outcome, and there is no direct RISK_APPROVED -> ACKNOWLEDGED rule, so the database would have refused a write the service believed it had made. Two transitions are recorded now, and SUBMITTING is recorded *before* the venue is called, so the interval between leaving the platform's control and learning the outcome is visible in the journal rather than indistinguishable from an order that was never sent.

The risk-reducing classification existed in four places (defect 42). contracts.OrderType.RiskIncreasing() is the one domain/gate calls and matches all nine values of common.order_type. Package oms carried a second type, with six of those nine, a RiskReducing() method documented as 'the same predicate migration 0013 uses at the risk boundary', a comment in domain/instrument citing it, and no consumer outside its own test -- so the function the tests exercised was not the function deciding anything, and its own test passed while listing only the members it happened to mention. oms.OrderType is deleted, instrument's closing() delegates to contracts, and the parity test reads contracts.

IOC and FOK appeared in both common.order_type and common.time_in_force (defect 43). oms.order holds both columns NOT NULL and no constraint prevented a contradictory pair, so order_type='IOC' with time_in_force='GTC' was accepted and read two ways. Migration 0022 forbids them in oms.order.order_type. Dropping the enum values was rejected as destructive: market.instrument.order_types and risk.policy.permitted_order_types are arrays of common.order_type and may legitimately list them as venue capabilities.

Two of the fourteen event kinds drive no transition (defect 44). SUBMIT_FAILED and CANCEL_REQUESTED cannot move an order. That is legitimate -- the enum is shared with the journal -- but it was unrecorded, and a kind that looks actionable while being inert is the shape of a control nobody calls. Now pinned by name, so a third inert kind fails and a kind that starts driving a rule must be removed from the list.

The risk gate's control enumeration was pinned only by count. TestTheGateEvaluatesExactlyDoc04sFifteenControls asserted that fifteen controls run, and TestColumnsWithNoDoc04Control pinned the policy columns to the controls, and the parity test pinned the projection to information_schema -- but all three iterate whatever Controls() returns, so every one of them is consistent with a control having been removed. Which fifteen controls those were, and that they were doc 04's fifteen in doc 04's order, existed only as a prose comment at risk.go:370. CLOSED: both doc04_test.go files read doc 04 at test time and assert the mapping in both directions.

The composed gate asserted it had checked halts. gate.Evaluate passed risk.HaltDecision{Evaluated: true} -- a literal claiming an evaluation that had not happened, the same shape as the caller-asserted booleans in S11 and S12, and it meant KILL_AND_HALT_STATE reported PASS on a halted system (defect 39). domain/halt/loader.go now reads active halts from ops.halt per environment and per scope, refuses an unknown halt level as an error rather than ignoring it, and a read failure is a refusal rather than a clearance.

MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL was unreachable (defect 40). OrderFacts.Notional was left to the caller and then unconditionally overwritten with nil by riskstate.Build, so the control compared a limit against an unset pointer and could not refuse anything -- the defect 24 shape, once more, on the one control that most directly bounds a loss. Notional is now derived from the order's own quantity and price. A market order has no price at submission, so the field stays nil and the control denies; inventing a value would have made the bound unenforceable exactly where it matters most.

The composed gate had never been run (defect 41). Policy, halts, account, position, strategy and instrument state had each been tested in isolation and in a lower-level integration test, but no test had ever asserted they coexist correctly in one entry point. 7 composition tests now do, and the permissive case was deliberately converted into a denial test once it emerged that three controls cannot be satisfied by anything in this repository today.

Instrument eligibility and precision validity were caller-asserted booleans on risk.OrderFacts, so the gate could be told that an instrument the catalogue records as DELISTED was eligible, or that a quantity off the increment grid was precise, and it would agree -- and report INSTRUMENT_ELIGIBILITY and PRECISION_VALIDITY as checked (defect 37's precondition). CLOSED: riskstate.Load reads both from market.instrument via instrument.Evaluate and overwrites whatever the caller passed. 6 new database tests, each pairing a refusal with a permissive case so a control that refused everything would fail half of them.

risk.OrderFacts carried no Side. Nothing needed it while eligibility was a caller-supplied boolean, and instrument.Permits keys its shorting check on side == 'SELL', so a missing or misspelled side fell straight through it and an instrument that cannot be shorted would have permitted a short (defect 37). Field added, and instrument.Permits now refuses a side that is neither BUY nor SELL rather than treating it as a buy (defect 38). The check lives in Permits rather than in Evaluate so every caller inherits it.

contracts.Decimal.Div was wrong whenever the two operands carried different scales (defect 36). It computed a*10^guard/b on the reasoning that the denominator's scale cancels against the numerator's, which is true only when the scales are equal, so 1/0.1 came out as 1. The power of ten now goes to whichever side it belongs on. Two risk ratios divide unlike scales, so max_drawdown and max_concentration were being compared against a corrupted figure -- and at unequal scales the old code crossed the 'above 1' guard and errored, so the measurement could not be taken at all rather than merely being wrong.

domain/instrument did not compile. A stray package-level var calling a nonexistent accessor had been left between IncrementMultiple's doc comment and the function, which both broke the build and orphaned the comment. Removed; the package now has the 6 tests it never had, and the comment documents the divide-and-multiply formulation that replaced the coefficient test.

The risk gate had never approved an order in a real configuration - CLOSED. domain/riskpolicy loads a committed risk.policy row and dbtest approves an order from it, with a paired denial for every limit and allowlist.
G1 criterion 9 (domain tests): UNSUPPORTED -> SUPPORTED. 78 unit tests across domain/oms, domain/strategy, domain/halt, domain/risk, plus 6 Go/SQL parity tests, mutation tested 11/11.
common.new_canonical_id was not the Go bit layout. Closed by 0020. The prior 'by design; IDs are opaque' note was an untested assumption and was false.
occurred_at_ns / recorded_at_ns were unbound to their TIMESTAMPTZ columns. Closed by 0021, which also corrects the reversed decision recorded at 0009:216.
strategy.Rule was keyed on From alone and silently dropped 3 of 12 rules (defect 21). Fixed; TestMultiSuccessorStatesAreNotLosingRules names the affected states.
OrderFacts.DuplicateOrder had inverted polarity versus every other field (defect 22). Renamed NoDuplicateOrder.
TestRiskIncreasingTransitionsRequireADecision passed while asserting nothing (defect 23). Rewritten against a literal list, as was the dual-control test.
max_open_orders, max_orders_per_minute and max_cancels_per_minute were set-but-never-consulted (defect 24). RATE_AND_THROTTLE_LIMIT now compares the counts itself.

permitted_instruments and permitted_venues were unread, so a restrictive policy behaved unconditionally (defect 25). INSTRUMENT_ELIGIBILITY and VENUE_AVAILABILITY now require both the external fact and policy membership.
risk.Policy was an invented limit model never compared to the schema (defect 26). Replaced by a projection of the real columns, pinned against information_schema by dbtest/risk_policy_parity_test.go.
pgx stdlib returns a text[] column as a literal string, so scanning permitted_* into []string failed at runtime (defect 27). A hand-written Scanner now parses the literal.
Interval parsing left the plural 's' behind on '2 days', and array Value() lost double quotes (defect 28). Both fixed and unit tested.
Committed test rows outlived their tests and shadowed later runs via policy_active_scope_idx (defect 29). Fixtures now delete in t.Cleanup and each test allocates its own environment.
project.json carried a UTF-8 BOM, which tolerant JSON parsers accept and strict ones reject. Stripped; the ledger now parses under Python json.load.

Account and strategy facts reached the risk gate as caller-supplied booleans (defect 31 partially). domain/riskstate now reads risk.account_state, portfolio.position and strategy.strategy, and riskstate.Load is the entry point that reads all three.

Build computed AccountAuthorized and StrategyDeployed and then discarded them (defect 31), so ACCOUNT_AND_ENVIRONMENT_AUTHORIZATION and STRATEGY_DEPLOYMENT_STATUS reported 'not evaluated' and denied every order for the wrong reason.

Build left a caller's asserted measurement in place for any field it did not measure (defect 32) -- a flat book kept the caller's concentration -- while stamping provenance as if this package had sourced it. Every field is now assigned unconditionally, and an unmeasured one is cleared to nil.

The risk-gate integration fixture asserted leverage, drawdown, daily loss, exposure and concentration as Go literals while reading nothing (defect 33), so it tested that the gate evaluates numbers the test chose. It now builds instruments, orders, validated fills and positions, and measures them through the sanctioned loaders.
Load accepted a caller-asserted read stamp (defect 35). It now stamps AccountStateAsOfNs and LoadedAt from what it actually read, so a stale row cannot be stamped as fresh.

The durable exit from UNKNOWN did not exist, so a timed-out submission had no sanctioned way to become whole again (defect 47-49). Resolution was reachable only through the retired Submitter, which held no durable record and kept its history in a caller-supplied slice. Command.Resolve now reads execution.submission, refuses unless an attempt is genuinely undetermined, reads the venue record, and commits the outcome, the OMS transition, the audit record and the outbox row in one transaction. A submission is rewritten in place rather than appended, because a second row would present one send as two attempts and defeat the very counting the no-retry rule rests on. An unrecognised answer, or a venue that cannot be asked, leaves the order UNKNOWN rather than resolving it.

There were two implementations of the OMS submit/resolve lifecycle, one of them non-durable (defect 50). The Submitter called the venue inline, journalled through a Recorder interface, and accepted the prior attempt history from its caller -- so the no-retry rule could be bypassed by passing an empty slice, and an order could move with nothing committed to account for it. It also carried a second Resolve that duplicated the new durable one without its durability. It is deleted rather than repaired, together with the obsolete Venue and Recorder interfaces, because submission is outbox-driven now (doc 05: a dispatcher reads committed rows) and audit goes through audit.Appender. The ledger had already recorded it as "the second and weaker door"; that note is now closed rather than carried.

Command.Resolve reported a hardcoded State of ACKNOWLEDGED while its transaction correctly wrote REJECTED (defect 48). The returned struct lied about what committed, and a caller could have acted on a transition the database never accepted. Found by TestResolvingToARejectionUnblocksTheOrder, which failed on the assertion. commitResolution now returns the state it actually committed.

CLOSED for function bodies by db/verify-schema-live.ps1, which compares every function body the migration files define against pg_proc.prosrc in the live database and exits 1 on any difference. Measured drift=0 over 62 functions, and proven load-bearing by mutation: with oms.guard_submitting_order_has_outbox neutered the new gate reports LIVE_DRIFT and exits 1 while db/migrate.ps1 in the same state reports 'failures=0 drift=0'. The gap was real and reproduced: it let a neutered trigger function survive a full migration run unnoticed. What remains open is recorded separately as a residual, because function bodies are not the whole schema.

Migration 0024's stated justification that 'ops.outbox rows are never deleted -- nothing in this repository or its migrations issues a DELETE against them' was false, and a control resting on a false premise has a known hole. dbtest/dispatch_test.go issued exactly that DELETE, and because the 0024 trigger is on oms.'order' it never fired on the delete, so an order could be committed in SUBMITTING, have its outbox row deleted, and never be rechecked because later updates leave the state unchanged and return early. Migration 0026 closes it with a narrow BEFORE DELETE trigger on ops.outbox, and the contradiction in the migration comment is corrected in place rather than left standing.

Migration 0026 mentions CREATE INDEX three times but declares one index, because two of the occurrences are inside comments. Any index comparison reading the migration files as raw text is therefore poisoned at its inputs: the declared count reads 87 instead of 85, so a PARSE_INCOMPLETE fail-closed check would fire forever against a correct repository, and a name comparison would report two phantom indexes as missing. Closed by reading every migration through a lexical comment stripper before parsing. The stripper consumes each dollar-quoted region WHOLE, closing on a backreference to the opening tag, because matching the tag alone does not stop a regex scanner from resuming inside the body. That distinction was not theoretical: the tag-only version blanked real SQL comment lines inside function bodies, changed the bodies pg_proc.prosrc holds, and produced 31 phantom LIVE_DRIFT reports against a correct database. Verified by hash that stripping changes zero of the 66 parsed function bodies while reducing 0026 mentions from 3 to 1.

A RECORDED ANOMALY THAT WAS SIMPLY FALSE, closed by re-testing it instead of re-explaining it (defect 60). The known gap claiming that contracts.Decimal.Coef() at money.go:201 is exported but not resolvable by the compiler -- in-package or cross-package, on a clean build cache, for a selector on a variable -- does not reproduce. A probe package inside the module selecting Coef() on a Decimal variable, which is the exact case the gap names as failing, compiles cleanly and prints 7; go build ./... and go test ./... are green. The cross-package half of the claim is falsified by that alone, so no toolchain anomaly needs to be invoked to explain anything. This is recorded because the general failure is worth more than the instance: a gap file is a claim, and a claim that has been measured once and never re-measured decays into folklore. Two of the 37 known gaps were stale in this way, and this one was the more dangerous of the two, because a compiler anomaly attributed to no known cause invites a workaround rather than a re-test.

The gate that verifies the schema was reading the schema's files in the wrong order (defect 61). db/verify-schema-live.ps1 walked each migration with two grouped passes -- every CREATE TRIGGER first, then every DROP TRIGGER -- and migration 0026 drops and recreates ops.outbox.ops_outbox_delete_preserves_submitting_order inside a single file so that its no-transaction migration converges however many times it is applied. The trailing DROP therefore erased a declaration the same file had made moments earlier, and the gate reported a trigger as MISSING from a database that held it. The symptom looked like a live drift on a healthy database, and the first instinct -- to distrust the database -- would have been exactly wrong. Statements are now walked in file order, and T5 in the mutation harness is the negative control that pins it: T1-T4 all mutate the live database and every one of them passes against the broken parser as well, so without T5 the fix could have been reverted without any test noticing.

A verifier's own text can poison its inputs, and the wording of the fix is part of the contract (defect 62). Migration 0027 ends with a DO block whose RAISE EXCEPTION message explains how to recover from an index left INVALID by an interrupted concurrent build, and that explanation contained the words CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX inside a string literal. db/verify-schema-live.ps1 counts declared indexes with a regular expression that does not parse string literals -- a deliberate simplification, since deparsing makes predicate comparison unreliable -- so the message registered as two more declared indexes that no statement matched, and the parse-completeness cross-check fired PARSE_INCOMPLETE forever against a correct repository. A fail-closed check that fires on correct input is worse than no check, because it trains its reader to ignore it. The message is now phrased around the index name, and the comment in the migration says why. The general form: a file read as text by a verifier is an input contract, and prose inside it is not free.

A comment stripper is not enough when the verifier also has to read string literals (defect 62, second half). The same gate already strips comments lexically, consuming each dollar-quoted region whole with a backreference to its opening tag, which was added for exactly this reason. Comments were solved and literals were not, which is the more surprising half: a reviewer reading the migration would see one CREATE INDEX, and the gate would see three. M7 catches the comment case and the 0027 case is the literal case, so the harness now demonstrates both.

F4 (function dimension, PARSE_INCOMPLETE) reported NOT DETECTED for three consecutive runs and was mislabelled as a detector gap. Resolution 2026-10-03: the detector was correct and the FIXTURE was wrong. The gate's function pattern requires a dollar-quoted body and has no semicolon requirement, so the fixture's semicolon-less declaration parsed normally; the gate then reported all three sandbox functions MISSING_IN_DATABASE and never reached the under-parse check. Replacing the fixture with a single-quoted body produces the expected message: 'declare 3 CREATE [OR REPLACE] FUNCTION statements but only 2 could be parsed', exit 1.

REVIEW DISPOSITIONS 2026-10-03, all verified rather than assumed. Fixed: the docs/26 hex rule is now scoped to the function dimension instead of claiming it for the harness; this file's '9 of 9' tally is corrected to 8 of 8 (five function cases plus the three-case transport self-test), which reconciles with the case-counting convention used by the other schemaGate entries; F2's dollar sign is recorded as being in the function SIGNATURE rather than its body; F4's parsed count is pinned to exactly 2 instead of merely 'fewer than 3'; and an unreadable prosrc after a restore is now an explicit failure rather than a $null -eq $null pass. Rejected: the reviewer's claim that 73 of 74 bodies begin with a newline, because the measured figures are 55 of 63 beginning and 63 of 63 ending. Re-verified after every fix: 25 of 25 assertions with not_detected=0, gate drift=0, migrate applied_now=0 drift=0.
methodNotes: A severity is a claim about reachability, and a reviewer's severity is a hypothesis. All three CRITICALs in the uncommitted review were investigated before anything was changed and all three were downgraded to WARNING: 0009 and 0013 had no non-local environment to affect (every DSN in the repository is localhost:55439, there is no CI workflow, no Dockerfile and no migration runner outside db/migrate.ps1, and infra/ is documentation and alert rules only), and evaluateEligibility's fail-open is reachable only from tests because gate.Evaluate has exactly seven callers, all in dbtest, and Command.Prepare only requires a RiskDecisionID that already exists. Investigation cost one round trip and changed the plan; assuming the review's own framing would have meant a destructive local reset justified by a production risk that does not exist.

Two of the four warnings under remediation cited paths that do not exist (db/store.go, db/reconcile.go; the real files are domain/execution/store.go and services/reconcile/reconcile.go), and the fourth -- RecordAttempt is dead code -- was false, because four dbtest callers reference it. A finding was verified against the code before it was acted on, and that check turned a proposed deletion into a no-op. Under-reporting a review is cheaper than deleting a symbol four tests call.

Stale database state is not an encoding defect, and the way to tell is to measure the transport rather than reason about it. The section signs in three 0017 functions were '?' in prosrc after a -Reset, which reads exactly like the ASCII pipeline bug migrate.ps1 documents at length. Piping a section sign through the identical path returned ascii 167, a plpgsql function created through that path stored the character intact, and re-creating the three functions through it restored real section signs -- so the transport was never broken and the bodies on disk were stale. Two further repairs followed from the same lesson: DROP FUNCTION ... CASCADE silently removed the two dependent triggers, which the gate then reported as MISSING_TRIGGER, so a repair that works can still leave the schema worse than it found it. The gate caught both, which is the argument for running it after a repair rather than assuming the repair was complete.

A review that finds two instances of a defect has not established that there are two. The uncommitted review reported two per-row query loops in services/reconcile, at checkFills and checkPositions, and both were batched into single grouped reads. checkBalances was left as an unaudited known gap rather than assumed clean, and when it was finally read it carried the identical shape: one QueryRowContext per currency. All three checks now batch, each keyed on a UNIQUE index that makes the grouped read unable to collapse two rows into one. The lesson is that the count in a finding is a lower bound, and an unreviewed sibling of a reviewed defect is an unexamined defect.

A skipped suite is not a passing suite, and a green package line is not evidence that its tests ran. `go test ./...` printed ok for github.com/aitc/trade/dbtest in 2.7s while actually reporting 18 PASS and 364 SKIP, because dbtest skips rather than fails when AITC_TEST_DATABASE_URL is unset (dbtest.go:11). Count PASS and SKIP from a -v run before quoting any total. The 953 figure requires the DSN set AND exclusive database access; without the DSN the suite reports ok and means nothing.

Two concurrent test runs against one development database deadlock each other, and the failure lands in cleanup rather than in the assertion under test. 17 reconcile and execution tests failed on 'truncate after committed test: ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01)' at dbtest.go:115 because a second `go test ./dbtest/` was started against the same container while the first was still running. The symptom reads exactly like a regression in the code just edited, and it was not one: not a single assertion failed. Run one suite at a time against a shared database, and check pg_stat_activity before believing a mass database failure.

A uniform failure across one package in seconds rather than minutes is infrastructure, not a defect. 253 dbtest tests failed together in 2s because Docker Desktop had exited and the container was down; the pure-Go packages all passed. Check the container before reading a mass failure as a code change, and say which it was.

A sequencing rule cannot live in a state machine or a schema. The no-retry-after-UNKNOWN requirement has a legal transition, a legal row, and no enforcement anywhere, because every layer that could see it sees only part of the fact: the adapter caused the timeout, the gate evaluates an unsubmitted order, and a CHECK sees one row rather than the history of sends. Sequencing constraints need a layer whose unit of work is the sequence.

Let the closed set reject the draft. The orchestrator's first version recorded a single RISK_APPROVED -> ACKNOWLEDGED move, and the state machine refused it at runtime -- which is what a closed set transcribed from a specification is for. Writing the transition down without checking it would have produced a journal entry the database then refused.

A test that lists the members it happens to mention cannot notice a member it omits. TestRiskReducingClassificationIsExactlyTheTwoOrderTypes named four of nine order types and passed for as long as it existed; the same shape let a six-member vocabulary sit beside a nine-member one.

A mutant that fails to compile proves nothing about the mutant. The first attempt at disabling the no-retry guard unbalanced a block and broke the build; that is a broken harness, not evidence, and the anchor was rewritten to compile before the result was believed.

Pin a derived table's alphabet, not just the derivation. oms.state_transition_rule was compared to the Go rules on every run, so a rule row is a checked fact -- but every rule row names two states and an event kind, and nothing compared those vocabularies to their enums. That gap is precisely why a six-member order-type set could sit inside package oms disagreeing with a nine-member enum for as long as it did: the tests were looking at the wrong table.

An enum value is not a defect; two columns able to express the same instruction is. IOC and FOK are legitimately in both common.order_type and common.time_in_force, and legitimately listable in the instrument and policy arrays. The defect was only that oms.order let a single row carry the instruction twice with nothing stopping the two from contradicting.

Test the classification that decides, not a copy that documents it. oms.OrderType.RiskReducing() was mutation-tested against the database and cited by two other packages as the risk-boundary predicate, while domain/gate called contracts.OrderType.RiskIncreasing() instead. A predicate's importance is a function of what calls it, and coverage of the unused copy is worse than no coverage: it reads as evidence.

A search that finds nothing is a fact about the search until the negative is re-derived. Searching the docs for the 15 control identifiers returned no matches, which looked like proof the control set was invented; doc 04 states its checks in prose ('notional limits', not MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL). Separately, a grep reporting all 12 policy limits unread was wrong because it omitted the file that reads them -- a false defect is as costly as a missed one, so re-derive a negative before recording it.

Pinning a count is not pinning a set. Three separate tests asserted that fifteen controls run and that each policy column is mapped, and every one of them iterates Controls(), so all three would have passed with a control deleted. Completeness needs a test that compares against the specification itself.

A test that reads its authority from disk must fail when the authority is missing. Skipping on an unreadable doc would leave the gate unpinned in precisely the checkout that lacks the specification, and a skip reports as a pass.

A control reported as evaluated must have been evaluated. `Halt: risk.HaltDecision{Evaluated: true}` reads as a decision and is not one: it is the same assertion pattern as the caller-supplied booleans, written inline where the compiler cannot see it and no test can cross-check it. Every Evaluated/Established flag needs a data dependency, not a literal.

A mutation that leaves the suite green is a finding about the code, not the mutant. Disabling the early halt return changed nothing because the recheck enforces the same condition independently -- which is the redundancy the design intended, and which no test would have revealed without the mutant.

A test that expects approval where the system can only deny is not a strict test, it is a wrong one. The permissive composition case was rewritten to assert the denial names exactly the three unsourceable controls, so it fails loudly when reality improves instead of passing vacuously either way.

A control keyed on a field the struct does not have fails open. The shorting check is written as side == "SELL", so a missing Side reads as a buy rather than as an error; every field a guard depends on needs its own validity check, and an absent value must refuse rather than fall through.

A fixture that asserts the fact under test is what made instrument eligibility look covered. Load must read it from the row, overwrite the caller's value, and be tested by changing the catalogue -- including a test where the caller claims the opposite and must lose.

A division is only as correct as the relationship between the two scales it is handed. A formula that folds the divisor's scale away is right for every test case whose operands happen to share a scale, which is why the defect survived a suite of 400 tests.

A green integration suite does not mean the arithmetic is pinned. Reverting Div left dbtest entirely green while four unit tests failed: the fixture's operands shared a scale. When a control's correctness lives in arithmetic rather than in a row, the unit test has to choose operands the fixture would never produce.

An integration fixture that supplies the fact under test repeats the defect it was written to catch. dbtest still asserts InstrumentEligible and PrecisionValid as literals, and domain/instrument -- which reads the real rows -- has no caller at all. A package that answers the question correctly and is never asked it is indistinguishable, from the outside, from a package that does not exist.
Mutation testing is load-bearing: four controls were found carried by a caller higher in the call path, or written and never invoked.
Defect pattern 14 (schema comments asserting enforcement that does not exist) has recurred across the migration set.
Tests that pass when their control is deleted are worse than no test; isolate a control's own contract directly.
A guard that exists and is never called is the same failure as a guard that is a comment: it provides the appearance of a control and none of the effect.

When a consistency check appears to produce false positives, suspect the callers before deleting the check. A check that fires on correct data is a finding about the callers, not grounds for removing the mechanism.
A mutation result that disagrees with a direct check is a question about the harness, not the mutant. Re-derive rather than accepting the first number.
Inline digests in a report that quotes the digested file are stale on contact. Generate them and verify them instead.
Two domain tests derived their expectations from the table under test and passed vacuously under mutation. Write the specification out literally and compare.
A mutation caught only by a compile error is weaker evidence than one caught by a named test; prefer single-line anchors that still compile.

A column an operator can set and believe is enforced is a live hole, not a documentation gap: max_open_orders and permitted_instruments were both readable, settable, and consulted by nothing. Enumerate the schema's columns and assert every one is either read or recorded as a gap.

A driver returns types in the shape it chooses: pgx stdlib hands back a text[] as a literal string, so a []string destination fails at runtime on the first array column read. Read the driver's actual behaviour before assuming a scan target.
A test fixture that commits leaves residue, and residue makes the second run a different test. Run the suite twice consecutively and assert the tables are unchanged.
Constraint checking is not ordered by name. A row invalid for two reasons reports an arbitrary one, so a test asserting a specific constraint must make the row valid for every other constraint.

A test that supplies the measurements it is checking proves the checker works on the test's numbers. When a control's inputs live in a table, the fixture must write and read that table even at the cost of a long setup.

The schema refusing a short fixture is evidence, not an obstacle. Three refusals (a fill watermark no fill backed, a quantity validated fills did not imply, an order inserted straight into FILLED) each replaced a claim with a derivation.

A checked constraint is also an immutability guarantee, and immutability removes cleanup-by-DELETE. When a fixture must insert immutable rows, it belongs in a transaction that rolls back; that requires the loader to accept a querier rather than a *sql.DB.

A context passed to BeginTx must outlive the transaction. Cancelling it with a defer inside the constructor that began it kills the transaction on return, and the failure surfaces far from its cause, as 'transaction has already been committed or rolled back' from the next unrelated query.
A narrow -run filter reports nothing about the tests it did not select. A subtest group can look green in isolation because its pattern never matched; run the full suite before believing a filter.

A computed value that is used to make a decision and then dropped is a control that never reports. Build refused on a non-deployed strategy without recording the fact, so the gate saw no fact at all and denied for the wrong reason.

Two implementations of a money-affecting operation are worse than one weak implementation. The durable Resolve was added while the Submitter still carried its own Resolve, and for a moment the package held two ways to resolve an order -- one of which silently wrote nothing durable. Deleting the superseded path was part of completing the new one, not follow-up cleanup.

A mutation that does not apply is indistinguishable from a mutation the tests do not catch. Disabling Resolve's guard reported green; the replacement string had been written against a one-line form while the code used a two-line form, so the file was byte-identical afterwards. The earlier lesson -- a mutant that fails to compile proves nothing -- has a symmetric twin, and both are caught the same way: assert that the anchor changed before believing the result.

A returned struct must report what committed, not what the function intended. The hardcoded ACKNOWLEDGED was invisible to every test except the one that happened to resolve to a rejection, because for the common case the intended value and the committed value agreed. Returning the state from the transaction is what makes the disagreement impossible rather than merely untested.

A shared deterministic identifier makes a test file's position in the alphabet load-bearing. dbtest.CanonicalID mixes a per-run nonce with the n passed in, so two call sites passing the same n produce the same primary key; and where a fixture must observe a real commit against an append-only table, the rows it wrote cannot be rolled back, so its ids outlive it. Most files then rely on their literals being safe because their inserts DO roll back -- a correctness property of ordering that nothing states and nothing enforces. The symptom was thirteen failures in three files, none of which touched the new code, each reporting a duplicate key rather than an id collision. When a change to one test file breaks unrelated tests with a constraint violation, the first question is which range of the shared identifier space the new file claimed, not what the new file did wrong.

Prove a test-only change by removing it, not by reasoning about it. Thirteen failures across three files pointed at the dispatcher, and every one of them was exonerated by a single A/B run with the file moved out of the build. The reasoning that led there -- committed rows cannot be cleaned up, literals are only safe because they roll back -- was correct and was still worth nothing until it was converted into 333 pass / 0 fail versus 325 pass / 20 fail.

A restore can report byte-identical and not be. PowerShell Set-Content -Encoding utf8 writes a BOM, so the mutation harness that restored services/dispatch/dispatch.go after six mutations left a UTF-8 byte-order mark at the head of a Go source file, and Get-Content -Raw strips BOMs, so the harness compared the string and concluded the file was unchanged. It was not: gofmt flagged it and nothing else did. This is the same shape as the earlier lesson about a mutation that does not apply -- the check that validates the harness has to be the same kind of check as the one validating the work, and a string comparison cannot see a byte-order mark. The restore now writes through [System.IO.File]::WriteAllBytes with an explicit UTF8Encoding($false), and the BOM is asserted absent afterwards.

A hand-picked fixture can be vacuous, and a passing assertion over it proves nothing. The nonce constants for the sequence-namespace tests were chosen by eye, and 1<<30 masks to zero under (n & 0x3fffffff) % 100000 -- so it silently belonged in the COLLAPSED case while sitting in the list of DISTINCT ones. The test failed loudly, which is the only reason it was noticed. The fixtures are now found by searching for a desired multiplier rather than hardcoded, and every such test asserts the precondition it depends on: a fixture that stops being degenerate should say so rather than quietly stop testing anything.

A defect that fires once in a hundred thousand runs and then poisons the database forever will not be found by running the suite more times, which is the only tool the suite offers. Defect 53 was found by accident, after a run happened to land on a zero multiplier and left two rows that ledger.entry's append-only rule made permanent. The general move is to convert the rare case into a permanent one: set the input deliberately so the degenerate branch runs every time. Where an input cannot be set -- a clock the production code owns -- the rare case still has to be reachable by construction, and it now is, through SetRunNonce.

A fixture that reached past a guard it just added will not fail when the guard is wrong; it will fail when the guard is right, and the resulting noise reads as a defect in the new invariant rather than as the fixture having been built on a shape the schema now forbids. Migration 0024 broke 14 position-reconciliation tests the moment it applied, all through the shared MustOrderAt helper, which walked an order to SUBMITTING and wrote no outbox row because no such row had ever been required. The repair was to make the fixture do what Command.Prepare does -- write both halves of the pairing -- rather than to exempt fixtures, relax the trigger, or seed the state directly. The lesson generalises: when a new invariant lands, the first failures are usually the fixtures that were quietly violating it, and the honest response is to fix the fixture to satisfy the invariant, because the fixture is the code that was lying about what the schema permits.

The mutation harness has now failed to apply its mutation three separate times, in three different ways: a replacement string that did not match the two-line form it was written against (execution.resolveAndNoRetry), an uncompiled mutant that proved nothing (execution.noRetry), and PowerShell dollar-quoting mangled by docker exec -c so the SQL never reached the database (0024+0025). The first two failed loudly, or were caught by inspection; the third reported green, which is the dangerous version. The habit that catches all three is the same and costs one query: capture md5(pg_proc.prosrc) before, apply, capture again, and only trust a result once the two hashes differ. A green mutation test is not evidence until the mutation has been shown to exist.

A gate that under-reports what it examined is worse than no gate, because its green result is then read as coverage. db/verify-schema-live.ps1 shipped in this very session reporting 'expected_functions=62 drift=0' while the files declared 63 functions and the omitted one -- config.assert_no_embedded_secrets, whose signature contains a default of '$' -- was live holding a corrupted body. The defect was in the pattern, not in the schema, and it was invisible precisely because the gate printed its own parse count and nobody compared it to the declaration count. The cross-check that now exists (declared CREATE FUNCTION statements must equal parsed ones, or exit 1 with PARSE_INCOMPLETE) is the general form of the lesson: a verifier must prove it looked at everything it claims to have looked at, and must refuse to return a verdict when it cannot.

Do not write a schema literal you have not read from the schema. Three literals in this session were wrong on first use and each was caught by querying rather than reasoning: the canonical id prefix (canonical ids join the prefix to the entropy with an underscore, so 'ord_' not 'ord-'; the schema already states it as common.is_canonical_id(order_id, 'ord'), which should have been the first thing reached for), the event kind for a SUBMITTING -> REJECTED transition (SUBMIT_FAILED is refused; the rule table allows only REJECTED_BY_VENUE), and the order_event id prefix ('oe1', not 'oe9'). Each cost a failed migration or a failed test. The rule is simple and was violated three times: ask the constraint or the lookup table, never infer the value.

An independent verifier paid for itself immediately, and not decoratively. It returned FAIL against work that had just passed every gate this session had run, and its two HIGH findings were both about MY OWN claims: a third corrupted function the new gate was structurally blind to, and the fact that the encoding fix I had written and 'verified' set the wrong PowerShell variable entirely. Neither was visible from inside the work, because the gate reporting drift=0 was itself the defective instrument. The generalisable form: self-verification is weakest exactly where the instrument is shared with the work, so a control that was just built should be audited by something that did not build it, and any fix should be proven by a measurement that could have failed rather than by an absence of error output.

A probe against an empty table answers nothing, and it looks like an answer. Both "DELETE FROM oms.order" and "TRUNCATE ops.outbox" reported success against a database holding zero rows, which could have been reported as "the guard does not prevent either". TRUNCATE really does bypass the guard -- but the empty table hid the fact that DELETE of a protected row is refused, and hid it behind a green result. The re-run against a real committed order is what separated the two: DELETE refused, order-delete refused by foreign key, TRUNCATE allowed. The habit is the one already recorded for mutation harnesses, applied to destructive-operation probes: establish that the thing under test actually exists before concluding anything about what happens to it.

Two independent review delegations in this session both returned an empty result. Neither is reported as verification, and no finding is attributed to them. The verification that stands is self-performed and is recorded as such: the full suite run twice with identical results and zero residue, the PARSE_INCOMPLETE cross-check demonstrated to fire against an unparseable function in an isolated copy of the migrations directory, and the bypass probe run against real data. The useful lesson is about the earlier reviews rather than about these: the one that DID return a result found two HIGH defects that every self-run gate had missed, so an empty delegation is not a neutral event -- it is a missing input that has to be replaced by verification performed some other way, never by assuming the absence of findings.

MEASURE WHETHER A COMPARISON IS EVEN POSSIBLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING IT. The obvious implementation of an index gate is to compare the declared DDL against pg_get_indexdef. Measured against a correct database, that approach produces 38 false mismatches before it finds a single real one, for reasons that are properties of PostgreSQL deparsing rather than of this repository: DESC and NULLS ordering are absent from the per-column form, IN lists become = ANY (ARRAY[...]), and enum literals gain type labels. Writing the comparator first and then discovering it manufactures false drift would have shipped a gate whose failures could not be trusted. Measuring the comparability of each candidate fact first, where key count and column names both came back at 0 mismatches and predicate and sort direction did not, is what made the choice defensible, and it also produced the honest scope statement instead of a claim of coverage. The same discipline settled the other two questions this stage raised: whether index names are globally unique, which they are not, since state_transition_rule_pkey is in both oms and strategy and the live map is therefore keyed by schema and name; and whether a comment can poison a DDL count, which it can, and it already had.

A CLAIM IN THIS LEDGER WAS WRONG AND WAS FOUND BY ASKING GIT RATHER THAN BY REASONING. baselineCommit read b971dda, which is the commit before HEAD; the actual base every working-tree change sits on is 13a4a9c, dated 2026-09-30. The field was stale rather than falsified -- no work was done on the wrong base -- but a ledger that names the wrong commit cannot be used to ask what a given change was measured against, which is the only reason it is kept. The habit is the one already recorded for the Coef() anomaly: re-measure a standing claim instead of carrying it, because a claim that has been true once decays.

A GATE THAT HAS ONLY BEEN RUN AGAINST A CORRECT SCHEMA HAS BEEN SHOWN TO DO NOTHING. db/verify-schema-live.ps1 was green on every run since it was written, which proved only that it did not fail, not that it could detect. The index mutation proof is a committed script rather than an ad hoc session because that argument does not expire. Three separate defects were found by the proofs rather than by reading the code: the reporting line named the wrong property, so an undeclared index printed as "ops. on ops.outbox"; the restore path left the schema mutated twice, once because a repointed index still occupied its name and once because a benign NOTICE on stderr became a terminating error inside a finally and skipped the re-creation; and the comment stripper silently corrupted 31 function bodies. None of those is visible from reading the code, and the second would have been discovered by whoever ran the script next, against whatever database they cared about.

A NEGATIVE CONTROL IS PART OF THE PROOF, NOT A SEPARATE NICETY. The CONSTRAINT_NOT_VALIDATED mutation C3 passes against two very different gates: one that compares live validation against DECLARED validation, and one that flags every unvalidated constraint. Only a negative control separates them, so C5 asserts that audit.record.audit_signing_key_required -- genuinely unvalidated, deliberately declared unvalidated -- is NOT reported. A positive mutation that any stricter implementation would also catch proves nothing about which implementation is actually present. The general form: whenever a change is about not over-reporting, the mutation suite must include a case that a naive version of the same change would fail.

convalidated HAS THREE OUTPUT FORMS AND TWO OF THEM ARE WRONG FOR YOU. Selecting the raw boolean through psql -t gives the DISPLAY form t or f; casting to text gives true or false; casting to int gives 1 or 0. Comparing the raw form against 0 fails a correct result, and comparing a text cast against t reports every row as unvalidated -- which is exactly what happened here and produced 261 phantom NOT-VALID findings before any of it was written up. Cast to int in every comparison. Twice in this one feature the bug was in the check and never in the gate, which is the reason to distrust a finding before believing it, and the reason a mutation suite reports pass rates rather than a single verdict.

SPEED IS PART OF CORRECTNESS FOR A GATE THAT HAS TO BE RUN. Letting the constraint capture cross newlines fixed a silent 84-constraint under-count but pushed the gate past a 600s budget, at which point it is not a gate. Matching the type keyword directly in the pattern, instead of capturing the clause body and classifying it afterwards, is both the faster and the safer formulation: a fixed local match, and it excludes CONSTRAINT TRIGGER without a special case because TRIGGER is not one of the five keywords. Runtime went from over 600s to 39s on the same 262 constraints compared. When a fix trades accuracy against runtime, check whether the slower formulation was ever necessary instead of assuming the cost was inherent.

WHEN A PARSER CANNOT BE TRUSTED, INVERT THE TEST. The declared-side parser was verified from the LIVE side instead: cross-check every live constraint in the owned schemas against the declared set and account for every difference by name. Five remained unresolved and all five were constraint triggers already covered by the trigger dimension, which is a complete account rather than a shrug. Self-consistency of a parser against its own input proves only that it is consistently wrong; an independent direction can at least disagree, and here it disagreed usefully -- it is what exposed the newline bug that the parser own parse-completeness check had already passed.

A TRIGGER IS NOT A REGCLASS, AND THE CATALOG QUERY YOU REUSE IS NOT ALWAYS THE RIGHT ONE. The trigger mutation dimension began by calling the same 'schema.table.trigger'::regclass shape Get-IndexDef uses for indexes. It is a relation lookup, so it fails for every trigger; the helper swallowed the error and returned null, so the harness recorded every trigger as 'did not exist' and restored nothing. The first run left the live database one trigger short -- and the gate reported MISSING_TRIGGER, which is the detector working correctly on a schema the harness had broken. The failure had the best possible signature: the green path was silent and the broken path was loud, in a tool that exists to be loud. Two habits apply. A capture helper that returns null on error will convert any error into a confident 'this was never there', so the null case has to be distinguishable from the genuinely-absent case -- here by an explicit empty-string check. And a restore that is reached only on the happy path is not a restore.

A MEASUREMENT CAN CHANGE WHAT A QUESTION MEANS. G2 16c had been recorded for the session as an owner decision -- which market.freshness_policy row governs an order -- and that framing was correct as far as it went and implied a partial fix might be available meanwhile. Measuring instead of re-reading showed market.feed_health has no maintainer at all: zero Go references outside dbtest, zero rows, and its only trigger computes nothing. The partial fix was therefore not merely undesirable but strictly worse than the unconditional denial it would replace, because an aggregate over an empty table is either vacuously true (fail-open on its default state) or vacuously false (a refusal pointing at a table that is empty). The general form: before treating a blocked item as a decision pending, check whether the input the decision would select between is itself maintained by anything. A choice between undefined options is not a decision, and measuring that turned an owner question into a sequencing fact -- which also merged the G3 blocker and the G2 blocker into one item.

A GUARD ADDED TO A PROOF TOOL IS PART OF THE TOOL AND NEEDS ITS OWN PROOF. All three mutation dimensions now route their apply step through one helper that converts a failure to apply into a recorded NOT DETECTED instead of an exception that would abort the run -- a failure mode this harness had already hit four separate ways, once of which killed a run part-way through a dimension and silently skipped every case after it. A guard added on the reasoning that it obviously works would have been the exact mistake this file exists to prevent, so it is asserted by three self-test cases: valid SQL applies, invalid SQL is reported, and -- the one that protects the harness rather than reporting on it -- a benign NOTICE on stderr is not treated as a failure to apply. Without H3, every mutation that guards its own pre-drop with IF EXISTS would have been reported as not-applied, which is the same phantom-drift failure as a gate flagging 38 differences on a correct schema. The harness is now 20 of 20.

SUPERSEDED 2026-10-03. The harness is 25 of 25 across five dimensions, and the apply guard is reached through two helpers rather than one, for the transport reason recorded in verified.schemaGate.triggers. The reasoning in this note is unaffected and is the reason the self-test exists at all: a guard added to a proof tool is part of the tool and needs its own proof.

A RESTORE THAT FAILS INSIDE ITS OWN FINALLY PREVENTS ITS SIBLING STATEMENTS, AND A MUTATION THAT DOES NOT APPLY SHOULD BE A FINDING RATHER THAN AN ABORT. The trigger dimension's pre-drop used the qualified 'schema.table.trigger' form, which is a syntax error; the error was caught and recorded, but the re-create that followed was correctly skipped, so the trigger stayed dropped. Separately, T2's mutation SQL referenced a trigger name that does not exist (the real one is ops.outbox.outbox_principal_guard, not guard_principal_on_write), so the DROP TRIGGER raised, the exception propagated out of the harness, and the run died part-way through the dimension with T3-T5 never executed. Both are the same family as the three earlier 'the mutation did not apply' records, and the fix is the same shape as the existing one: an exception inside the mutation path is now caught, reported as NOT DETECTED with the psql error attached, and the run continues -- because a mutation that never reached the database has proved nothing about the detector, and reporting it as a pass is the one outcome that is worse than reporting it as a failure.

A MIGRATION EDITED AFTER IT HAS BEEN APPLIED IS A PERMANENT STATE UNLESS THE FILE IS RE-RUNNABLE, AND THE BLOCKER IS DUPLICATE OBJECT NAMES RATHER THAN ANYTHING TRANSACTIONAL. Appending a comment to 0019 left the live schema correct and the digest check reporting drift=1, and the tempting repairs were both wrong: re-recording the digest destroys the only evidence that the file and the ledger ever disagreed, and re-applying as written fails because CREATE TRIGGER and ADD CONSTRAINT against an existing name are hard errors. 0019 was transactional, so a failed re-apply would have rolled back whole and left nothing behind -- which means the failure was bounded, not catastrophic, and the fix was mechanical: precede each of its three trigger creations and two constraint additions with DROP ... IF EXISTS. The re-apply then took 2293 ms of real work and a second run reported applied_now=0, so re-runnability is demonstrated rather than assumed. The finding that matters beyond 0019 is that this is not a property of that one file: 34 object creations across the migration set have no preceding drop, so most applied migrations are not re-runnable as written and the same trap waits in each of them. A lint is the wrong answer today because it would fire 34 times, so the proportionate action is to make the tool that reports drift also report the recovery procedure -- including the one repair that must not be chosen. What generalises: a tool that detects a problem but leaves the repair to improvisation converts a detected fault into an unrecoverable one, and the recovery procedure belongs next to the detector because that is the only place the person holding the fault will look.

A JSON ROUND-TRIP THROUGH WINDOWS POWERSHELL SILENTLY DROPS KEYS CONTAINING A DOT, AND A FILE EDITED THAT WAY PRODUCES NO ERROR OF ANY KIND. Updating project.json by reading it with ConvertFrom-Json and writing it back with ConvertTo-Json removed verified['schemaGate.indexes'], verified['schemaGate.triggers'] and verified['schemaGate.constraints'] -- roughly 4000 characters of mutation-proof evidence -- while leaving the rest of the file valid, correctly shaped, and smaller than before. Two other dotted keys, dispatch.unitTests and dbtest.sequenceNamespace, survived, so the loss was partial and specific rather than a clean prefix or suffix, which is precisely why it would have been missed: nothing warned, and the file looked healthier than it was. It was caught only because a later lookup used dot notation, $j.verified.schemaGate.triggers, which returned nothing and looked like a PowerShell quirk rather than data loss -- and the first instinct, to consult Python for an authoritative view, is what distinguished the two. The lesson is not that PowerShell is unsafe but that a serializer must never be trusted to be lossless on a record whose whole purpose is to be durable, and that a suspiciously clean round-trip deserves a key count taken before and after. This project has now been bitten by the same family three times -- a UTF-8 BOM written by Set-Content, ANSI mis-decoding by Get-Content, and this -- all of them silent, and all of them in the same direction: a gate or ledger that reads as complete while having lost part of what it was asked to hold. Every write to this file from here uses Python's json module, and a key count is taken before and after.

A DOCUMENTATION CLAIM HAS TO BE VERIFIED AGAINST THE THING IT DESCRIBES BEFORE IT IS COMMITTED, AND ONE OF THE THREE FIXES WAS WRONG ON THE FIRST PASS. Writing docs/26 meant stating what migrations declare NOT VALID, and the draft said each such file records the VALIDATE CONSTRAINT statement to run after backfill. Grepping for it showed 0021 records six commented VALIDATE statements and 0023 records none, so the claim was false for one of the two files it described and was corrected to say so explicitly, including the consequence that retiring the signing-key constraint therefore needs a separate migration. Two related corrections came out of the same check: the draft described 0021's constraints loosely as timestamp bounds when there are six across five tables, and it did not warn that querying pg_constraint directly returns dozens of rows rather than seven, because audit.record is partitioned and each of its three unvalidated constraints is replicated onto all 15 partitions -- a reader who ran the query would have concluded the document was wrong. The general form is the one this project keeps relearning: a document describing code is a claim about code, and the cheaper it reads the more it needs checking, because the sentences that sound obviously right are the ones that were never run. It is also the mirror of the defect class recorded twice already here, where documentation asserted enforcement or coverage the code did not provide -- this time the documentation was the thing that was wrong, and only a direct query distinguished it.

OUT-STRING CORRUPTS VALUES AND CAN PRESENT AS A DETECTOR DEFECT. Measured on this host: a 300-char line through Out-String becomes 302 chars, because Out-String wraps at the console width (60 here, under powershell -File) and INSERTS newlines into the value it is meant to pass through. It broke the mutation harness twice, in two unrelated-looking ways, and both were initially misread as the gate failing to detect things. (1) It formatted a 1802-char hex string into 1832 chars, so a correctly restored 901-byte body was reported as 916 bytes and the restore check failed on a byte-perfect restore. (2) It formatted the GATE's text in Invoke-Script, splitting the long PARSE_INCOMPLETE sentence across lines so that no single-line pattern could ever match it -- while every case whose expected pattern was short kept passing and hid the cause entirely. The lesson generalises past this harness: when a comparison disagrees with a measurement, suspect the measurement's plumbing before suspecting the thing being measured, and check whether a positive control that shares the plumbing still passes. Every wrapper in the harness now joins psql's lines with a newline instead. Out-String must never be reintroduced there.

NEVER READ A FUNCTION BODY WITH 'SELECT p.prosrc' WHEN THE BYTES MATTER. Invoke-SqlBytes ends in .Trim(), so that read returns something that looks like the body and is not: this repository's function bodies begin and end with a newline, so it returned 901 characters for a 903-byte prosrc, and a restore spliced from it silently dropped two bytes. Read the body as hex and decode it -- hex has no whitespace to normalise and no line to break. A restore is verified by comparing hex, never by comparing trimmed strings, which is the whole reason Get-FunctionBodyHex exists.

NEVER READ A FUNCTION BODY WITH 'SELECT p.prosrc' WHEN THE BYTES MATTER. Invoke-SqlBytes ends in .Trim(), so that read returns something that looks like the body and is not: bodies in this repository end with a newline and 55 of the 63 non-empty ones also begin with one, so it returned 901 characters for the 903-byte prosrc of market.guard_feed_sequence_monotonic, and a restore spliced from it silently dropped two bytes. Read the body as hex and decode it -- hex has no whitespace to normalise and no line to break. SCOPE, corrected after independent review: this makes the function dimension verify a restore by comparing hex, never by comparing trimmed strings, which is the whole reason Get-FunctionBodyHex exists. It does NOT describe the index, constraint and trigger dimensions, which still compare deparsed definition strings; their definitions are single-line and unaffected by either hazard, but a multi-line or trailing-whitespace-bearing definition in those dimensions would need the same treatment. A blanket claim here would have told a future reader to audit three dimensions that were never converted.

CHARACTERS ARE NOT BYTES, AND IN A PROJECT WHOSE WHOLE POINT IS BYTE-EXACTNESS THAT IS A TRAP WORTH NAMING. Chasing an apparent discrepancy, the harness reported a function body as 2583 bytes while a direct query reported length(prosrc) as 2579, which looked like four missing bytes in a restore. Both numbers were right. PostgreSQL's length() counts CHARACTERS, and this body contains multi-byte UTF-8; encode(convert_to(prosrc,'UTF8'),'hex') counts BYTES, which is the number a byte-equality claim must use. md5 over the migration file's extracted body and md5(prosrc) matched, confirming the file and the database were byte-identical and that nothing needed fixing. The generalisation: a byte-exactness argument built on a character count is not a byte-exactness argument, and a surprising number is a reason to check the unit before hunting a defect. Two measurement errors in this session, both mine, came from the same place -- assuming a unit rather than reading it: a psql query using '\n' without the E'' prefix, which matches a literal backslash-n and reported every body as having no surrounding newline.

ONE COUNTER WAS DELIBERATELY NOT INCREMENTED. verified.fullSuiteGreenRuns stands at 30. This run is plainly another green full-suite run, so incrementing it to 31 would look like tidiness, but nothing in this file defines what qualifies as one -- not whether a run must follow a change, whether the database must be rebuilt first, or whether a re-verification counts separately from an incremental run. Inventing a counting rule to justify a number would put an unverifiable figure into the record, which is the failure this file exists to prevent. The re-verification is recorded in full under verified.fullSuiteReverifiedAfterDatabaseRebuild instead, where its date, command and figures can be checked.

A MUTATION SUITE THAT WAS GREEN FOR THE WRONG REASON, AND A GUARD THAT ONLY WARNED. db/mutate_domain.ps1 declared eleven domain mutations. Its last recorded clean run predates the restructuring of the risk comparison, so a run today would have reported ten of eleven and exited 1 rather than passing, because H's anchor no longer matched anything. Two of the eleven, K and I, were additionally reported caught while their MustFail patterns matched no test at all, so even those two were never verified to be caught for the reason they claim.

MUTATION H HAD NEVER EXECUTED. Its Find anchor was 'case cmp == 0 && limit.Boundary == BoundaryExclusive:' and its MustFail named BoundaryInclusivityDecidesTheExactLimitOrder. Neither string exists anywhere in the repository. The harness was not silent about this -- the pre-existing guard reports ANCHOR NOT FOUND and returns Caught=$false with Reason='anchor-not-found', so a run would have exited 1 -- but H had evidently not been executed since the risk comparison was restructured. A mutation that does not apply proves exactly as little as one that fails to compile.

THE REAL DESIGN IS NOT THE ONE H MUTATED. Boundary inclusivity is not decided by a switch over a Boundary value. domain/risk/risk.go fixes DerivationBoundary = BoundaryInclusive as a constant, and the inclusive semantics are baked into the comparison itself: measured.Cmp(bound) > 0 on the decimal path and measured > bound on the integer path, both in domain/risk/evaluate.go. BoundaryExclusive is declared and never consulted; risk.go says so in as many words, noting that only DerivationBoundary is currently meaningful. H was therefore mutating a decision no code consults, which is the same phantom-coverage shape the trigger dimension was found to have: an instrument reporting success while the thing it names is not exercised. H now flips the real comparison from > to >= and names TestBoundaryIsInclusiveAtTheExactLimit, and is caught by that test and by TestLimitComparisonsAreExactNotFloating.

RUNNING IT FOUND A WORSE DEFECT IN THE HARNESS. Mutations K and I were reported as CAUGHT while their MustFail patterns matched nothing at all. K's was UnmeasurableFigureDeniesDistinctlyFromAnUnconfiguredLimit, which is a description rather than a test name; the test that actually catches it is TestAnUnmeasurableFigureDeniesDistinctly. I's was UneaminedHaltGateRejects, a typo missing the v in Unevaluated; the test that catches it is TestAnUnevaluatedHaltGateRejects. Both mutations genuinely are caught, so the suite's headline count was not wrong about the mutants -- it was reporting caught without establishing that the assertion the mutation names is the one that failed. A mutation detected only incidentally, by some unrelated assertion that happened to break, satisfies none of the purpose.

THE GUARD THAT SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT THAT ONLY WARNED, and its message could not show what had mismatched. On a pattern matching nothing the script printed WARNING: expected a test named / pattern / to fail -- the literal characters / pattern /, because the message never interpolated $MustFailPattern -- then returned Caught = $true and exited 0. The domain harness was therefore strictly weaker than its SQL sibling db/verify-schema-live-mutations.ps1, which hard-fails the equivalent over-broad case. The wrong-reason branch now names both the pattern and the tests that did fail, or says plainly that no named test ran when the mutation failed to compile, and returns Caught = $false with Reason = 'wrong-reason', which the survivor accounting turns into exit 1. The survivor list no longer prints every unproven mutation as SURVIVED: only a genuine escape is called SURVIVED, and a wrong-reason or anchor-not-found outcome is reported as NOT PROVEN, because a report claiming a detected mutation survived would send an operator hunting for a missing test when the defect is a stale pattern or a name that no longer exists. A negative control was run to prove the new path fails correctly: the same K mutation with MustFail set to a name existing nowhere produced WRONG REASON: nothing mentions 'ThisTestNameDoesNotExistAnywhere', caught 0/1, exit 1. The identical case exited 0 before the change. All eleven now pass with no warning, and K and I are each caught by exactly the single test they name.

THE STALENESS WAS FOUND STATICALLY BEFORE ANYTHING WAS RUN, and the check itself was wrong twice first. Every literal mutation pattern in the six db/mutate_*.ps1 scripts was tested against its current target without touching the database or the working tree: 16 SQL patterns and 11 Go anchors, all matching. The five mutations in mutate_0020_0021.ps1 that build their pattern inside the script rather than as a literal are not statically testable at all and rest entirely on the in-script guard. Two preliminary versions of that check reported a stale pattern, and both were the checker's fault rather than the repository's -- one tested migration 0020's pattern against 0021 as well, because the -Target parameter rather than the pattern text decides which file a mutation is applied to; the other treated the replacement half of a -replace pair as if it were the pattern. Nothing in the repository was changed on the strength of either report. All six scripts carry a refuse-to-pass guard, and all five SQL ones additionally wrap the file write in a try/finally restore.

SCOPE, STATED PLAINLY SO IT IS NOT OVERCLAIMED. H now mutates the decimal comparison, which is the path all seven columns of TestBoundaryIsInclusiveAtTheExactLimit take. The integer comparison in evaluateRate, which serves CtrlRateLimit and is covered by TestCountsExactlyAtTheBoundAreWithinIt, is not separately mutated; it was not mutated before either, because H never ran. Closing that is a further mutation rather than a repair and is deliberately not claimed here. Every restore in the run was verified: gofmt reports the domain tree clean and git shows no modification to any Go file, so the eleven mutation runs left the sources byte-identical to the committed state. No production code changed, so the full-suite result recorded elsewhere still stands unrerun.

A CONCURRENCY ERROR IN THIS SESSION LEFT A MIGRATION MUTATED, AND THE ONLY THING THAT CAUGHT IT WAS git status. Two instances of db/mutate_0019.ps1 were run against aitc-pg17 simultaneously. The cause was mine: a follow-up call passed both a process id and a command to the process monitor, which started a second run rather than attaching to the first. Nothing in any of these harnesses prevents that. Each drops every schema and re-applies the whole migration series once per mutation, so two interleaved instances alternate DROP SCHEMA with CREATE, and each instance's finally-restore rewrites the migration file the other is midway through mutating.

THE SYMPTOMS WOULD HAVE BEEN EASY TO RECORD AS REAL FINDINGS, which is why they are written down. One mutation reported 'migration failed to apply -- relation public.schema_migration does not exist'. Another reported the SHORTING mutation as caught by TestAnInstrumentThatStoppedTradingIsRefusedAtRiskApproval, which is the TRADABILITY mutation's test. A third reported 'the mutation did not change the file -- the pattern did not match', which is exactly the message a genuinely stale anchor produces. All three are artifacts of the race and none is a property of the repository. Left unexamined, that run would have been filed as several migration defects, which is the overclaim this file exists to prevent.

THE DAMAGE WAS REAL. db/migrations/0019 was left mutated, because a finally block does not execute when a process is killed. It was reverted with git checkout, the database was rebuilt from scratch, and every check was re-run: applied_now=27 total_files=27 failures=0 drift=0; the live schema gate returned to drift=0 across 64 functions, 27 triggers, 85 indexes and 262 constraints; and the full Go suite against the rebuilt database reported 14 packages ok, 0 FAIL and 2 with no test files, matching the recorded baseline. The procedure is now written into docs/09 rather than left in a session: run exactly one instance, take no other action against the same database while it runs, and after any interruption treat git status on db/migrations as the first check rather than the exit code. A mutation claiming its pattern did not match should first be tested against a concurrent process rewriting the file.

RE-RUN ONE INSTANCE AT A TIME AGAINST THE REBUILT DATABASE. db/verify-schema-live-mutations.ps1: assertions=25 not_detected=0, OVERALL PASS, including all four negative controls (M7 an unparseable index, C5 a declared NOT VALID index, T5 a trigger dropped and recreated inside one migration, F5 a correct database reported clean) and the three-case H1-H3 self-test, ending with migrate reporting drift=0. db/mutate_0019.ps1: 8 of 8 caught, each by a distinct named test. db/mutate_0020_0021.ps1: 6 of 6 caught [A-F], each by a distinct named test. Both ended in RESTORED with the original bytes back and the schema rebuilt from them, and the schema gate was drift=0 and migrate applied_now=0 afterwards.

THE INTEGER HALF OF BOUNDARY INCLUSIVITY IS NOW MUTATED, RETIRING THE NON-CLAIM THIS FILE ITSELF MADE. The previous note recorded that mutation H covered the decimal comparison only, that evaluateRate's integer comparison serving CtrlRateLimit was not separately mutated, and that closing it was a further mutation rather than a repair. It is now H2: 'if measured > bound' becomes 'if measured >= bound', named TestCountsExactlyAtTheBoundAreWithinIt, and caught by exactly that test. Boundary inclusivity is mutation-proved on both the decimal and the integer path.

THE HARDCODED MUTATION COUNT IS NOW DERIVED. The script printed 'mutating 11 domain behaviours' as a literal, which is the stale-figure shape this file keeps finding: it drifted the instant a twelfth mutation was added and nothing would have reported the disagreement. It now reads the count from the array.

THE TESTING DOCUMENT DESCRIBED A STRATEGY THAT NEVER MENTIONED THE TECHNIQUE THE REPOSITORY ACTUALLY RELIES ON. docs/09_TESTING_AND_RELEASE_EVIDENCE.md was 28 lines of policy -- test pyramid, financial invariants, CI gates, release strategy, evidence package -- with no mention of mutation testing and no reference to any script in db/. The strongest verification evidence in the repository was reachable only from this file. It now carries the harnesses and their measured tallies, the three guarantees each harness makes, the role of the negative controls, and the fact that a killed run leaves a mutated migration behind.

THE PRIORITISATION WAS CORRECTED BY MEASURING WHICH MIGRATIONS HAD ACTUALLY MOVED, and the correction mattered. The first plan was to re-run mutate_0019 alone, reasoning that 0019 was the file edited during the drift repair. Checking when each migration was last touched showed that 0020 and 0021 were touched by the SAME commit dca8dfb on 2026-10-03, and that mutate_0020_0021 builds five of its six mutation patterns inside the script rather than as literals, making it the one harness whose anchors cannot be confirmed by reading the files at all. Had the original prioritisation stood, the single least verifiable harness in the set would have been the one left unproven. It was run: 6 of 6.

mutate_0016, mutate_0017 and mutate_0018 were left alone, and that is a measured decision rather than an assumption: all three were last touched on 2026-09-30, before the schema-gate work, and every literal anchor in their harnesses matches the current migration files. A static check can show that a mutation would still APPLY, never that it is still CAUGHT, so their tallies remain the ones recorded when they were measured. docs/09 states which tallies are current and which are historical instead of presenting one undifferentiated number.
